en: *Bhāruci’s Commentary on the Manusmṛti* (*Manu-Śāstra-Vivaraṇa*, Books 6–12), based on J. Duncan M. Derrett, *Bhāruci’s Commentary on the Manusmṛti*. 2 vols. Wiesbaden: Steiner, 1975.
D.

The first eight verses, which are missing in Derrett’s edition, are taken from *Bhāruci-praṇītaṃ Manuśāstravivaraṇam*, edited by S. Jagannatha. Oriental Research Institute, University of Mysore. Oriental Research Institute Series, 214. Mysuru: 2020. Edited by S. Jagannatha, Oriental Research Institute, University of Mysore, 2020.
M: Seventh Chapter.

M: Having thus established both the single-stage system (*ekāśramya*) and the four-stage system (*cāturāśramya*) along with their alternatives, [the author] now [proceeds] for the sake of protecting them.
I shall proclaim the duties of kings, how a monarch should conduct himself, how his origin comes about, and how his supreme success is achieved. (7.1)

M D: But the supreme success for a king consists in being accepted by the entire circle of kings; and subsequently, when he possesses sovereignty over the whole circle of the earth, there is the attainment of unsurpassed prosperity in the three goals of dharma, artha, and pleasure, as well as the excellence of his constituent elements such as the ministers and others. 7.1.
Having observed that this [duty] is accomplished therein, it is said:
"By a Kṣatriya who has received the Brāhmaṇical consecration according to rule, the protection of all this must be carried out in accordance with justice. (7.2)

The *brāhma* [sacrament] is the consecration (*saṃskāra*) for a Brāhmaṇa or belonging to a Brāhmaṇa, beginning with the initiation (*upanayana*) and ending with the ritual bath (*snāna*). By the phrase "by a Kṣatriya who has attained that," it is indicated that no other caste is meant. "According to rule" means according to the sacred texts. By the gesture expressed in the words "of all this," he points to those belonging to the castes and stages of life (*varṇāśramiṇaḥ*). "In accordance with justice" and "according to instruction" refers to the duty of protection; thus, the mention of "other occupations" is either an exclusive specification (*parisaṃkhyā*) or a restrictive injunction (*niyama*).

Some, however, consider that because its purpose is visible, the instruction [regarding the king's duties] is for the sake of livelihood; and if that were so, then upon the discovery of a treasure in ancestral wealth—which is not otherwise obtained—a Kṣatriya would not necessarily have to undertake the kingship. That is incorrect, because it has been stated: "The study of the Veda is for the Brāhmaṇa, protection for the Kṣatriya, and the work of trade for the Vaiśya; these are the specific duties among their own tasks" (MDh 10.80). Furthermore, the status of being "specific" for these duties is appropriate through their connection to both visible and invisible results. And the connection with the invisible result consists in the reliance upon the restrictive rule (*niyama*).

(D) Those who are without means of subsistence, helpless, and miserable are protected by the king; for protection is not merely for the sake of visible worldly benefit. Even for a *kṣatriya* who is not a king, there is the maintenance of fear through the praise of the restrictive rule (*niyama-śāstra*) which is meaningful even in the context of protecting villages and the like. Now, this is stated: (M) those without means of subsistence, as well as ascetics, the miserable, the helpless, and so forth—even for a *kṣatriya* who is a king, in the protection of villages and the like—this restrictive rule becomes meaningful with respect to them. Now, the cause for the origin of kingship is stated. || 7.2 ||
For when this world was without a king and everyone fled in fear from every side, the Lord created a king for the sake of protecting all this. (7.3)
(D) "Hiraṇyagarbha"—let there not be the "law of the fish" (*mātsyanyāya*). By this, the origin of the king for the sake of protecting subjects is demonstrated.
(M) "Let there not be injustice toward the subjects"—for the purpose of preventing that, the origin of the king is demonstrated by this.
(M D) This is a praise of the preceding injunction. 7.3.
Having extracted the eternal particles from Indra, Anila, Yama, and Arka; from Agni and Varuṇa; and from Candra and Vitteśa—7.4.

Regarding the injunction "Even a child must not be despised" (MDh 7.8), these ten verses that are about to be stated should be understood as supplementary to that [injunction]. Thus, it is said that he is fashioned from their constituent parts (mātrās) by means of that through which Indra and the others perform their activities within their own respective domains. 7.4.
Since the king was fashioned from portions of these lords of the gods, he therefore overcomes all beings with his splendor. (7.5)

The commentary (M D) states: By this purpose he demonstrates this meaning. Because, through sovereign power and lordship, he overcomes all beings by his own splendor, he is praised as being fashioned from the very essence of deities such as Indra. (7.5)
And because: It scorches both eyes and minds like the sun; and no one at all on earth is able even to look upon it. (7.6)

M D: Endowed with the insignia of a great king—such as the fly-whisk, the parasol, and the water-pot—he, by virtue of his brilliance, scorches the eyes like the sun, and [he torments] the minds through the infliction of punishment. Because of this, no one is even able to look upon him, much less do him harm. As before, this verse is also for the purpose of praise. 7.6.
And this being so, for the sake of accomplishing various tasks in those respective states:
he becomes fire and he becomes wind; he is the sun, he is the moon, and he is the King of Justice (Yama);
he is Kubera, he is Varuṇa, and by his power he is the great Indra. (7.7)
And thus are these world-protectors (lokapālas), by whom this king is likewise designated. 7.7.
M D: Since this is so, therefore:
"A king must not be despised even if he is a child, thinking 'he is but a man';
for he is a great deity dwelling in human form. (7.8)
For even a child can be turned away from doing what should not be done by means of ministers and others. 7.8.
Moreover:
"Ordinary fire burns only the man who approaches it carelessly;
but the fire of a king burns the entire family, along with its livestock and accumulated wealth. (7.9)
M D: Because he burns the family of those who commit an offense, as well as their accomplices and those connected to that transgression—for this reason also, he is not to be despised. || 7.9 ||
And because: "Having duly considered the task, his own power, and the place and time, he repeatedly assumes various forms for the sake of accomplishing dharma. (7.10)
Therefore, he should not be disregarded on account of his being a favorite, nor because of his friendship, nor by way of his kinship or benevolence. 7.10.
And because, when he was properly served:
"In whose favor dwells the lotus-born Śrī, in whose prowess victory, and in whose anger death; for he is composed of all splendor. (7.11)

Therefore, he is not to be propitiated merely out of fear for the sake of avoiding transgression; for from him, when properly served, there arises even spiritual prosperity (*abhyudaya*) that is distinguished [from mere freedom from harm]. || 7.11 ||
And this being so:
"But he who hates him out of delusion perishes without a doubt.

This refers to one who, disregarding the instruction as it was spoken, repeatedly [harbors ill will] because he does not hate him for the sake of another's offense—that by which [he might be destroyed].

M: As it has been said: "Since one should not feel resentment toward another even when faced with repetition, otherwise the king, due to that accumulation of offenses, will quickly set his mind upon one's destruction. (7.12)

D: But another person, when being hated, might sometimes endure it out of regard for *dharma* or due to incapacity; however, for the king who endures [the hatred], there is an independent contradiction, because he is capable of carrying out punishment. Therefore, he must always be followed by virtuous men free from guile. M: But another, being hated by him, even then—[nevertheless]—might endure it out of regard for *dharma* or due to incapacity; however, for the king who endures [the hatred], there is an independent contradiction, because he is capable of acting after having restrained [the offender]. Therefore, he must always be followed by virtuous men free from guile. (7.12)
Therefore, O lord of men, one should not question that law which the king ordains for those he favors, nor that which he ordains as unfavorable for those he disfavors. (7.13)

M: Indeed, the king is not the cause for the engagement in the duties of the castes and stages of life (*varṇāśramadharma*), because dharma and adharma are characterized by the sacred scriptures (*śāstra*). Furthermore, there would be a lack of order (*avyavasthā*) in this way; and there must be a scripture that establishes such order. Moreover, it has been stated many times that [the king's role] is for that purpose, and it would be improper to contradict that. Therefore, it should be understood from the context that this is primarily intended as praise of the king. With regard to worldly duties, this scripture is to be understood as the Veda. The origin of the king is concluded. 7.13.
Now, punishment, which is its auxiliary, is explained:
For the sake of that [dharma], the Lord first created Punishment, the son of Dharma, the protector of all beings, consisting of the splendor of Brahman. (7.14)

M.D.: From this point forward, twelve verses concern the origin of the rod of punishment (*daṇḍa*). Before the origin of kingship, he created his own son, Dharma, who is named the rod, consisting of splendor, and the protector of all beings. This is what is meant: "Without the rod, the state of kingship does not prevail; therefore, since there would be no such thing as kingship without the application of the rod, he created him [Dharma]. By means of this, the king will protect his subjects. (7.14)
And because: "All beings, both stationary and moving, out of fear of him perform their duties and do not deviate from their own nature. (7.15)

D: And he is born endowed for the assistance of the King, out of fear of whom even immobile things provide enjoyment through their fruits, shade, and so forth—how much more so other beings? For whatever immobile tree does not provide enjoyment, one certainly begins its clearing and so on; and since it is not cleared, it is abandoned and turned into charcoal. Furthermore, against that which acts in opposition, punishment is indeed inflicted through cutting, uprooting, and the like, just as in the case of a clump of *vīraṇa* grass and such grown upon a royal highway.

M: Therefore, this [punishment] is associated with the quality of passion (*rājasa*). Out of fear of that punishment, even immobile things become fit for enjoyment through their shadows and so forth; how much more so other [mobile beings]? An immobile tree becomes fit for enjoyment. He certainly undertakes its purification and so forth. And he who destroys it excessively is made to carry a load of rags (*kaṇṭhābhārī*). And for one who acts in opposition, there is cutting down; punishment is inflicted by uprooting, felling, and so on—just as a king [inflicts it] upon a clump of *vīraṇa* grass and the like belonging to the species of rabbits and such. || 7.15 ||
Having truly considered the place, the time, the power, and the learning [of the offender],
he should appropriately apply [punishment] toward men who act unjustly.

The place consists of villages, forests, the interior, the exterior, the streets, and so forth. The time consists of day and night, and [the state of being] a child, a youth, or an elder. Power consists of that pertaining to the body and that pertaining to wealth. Knowledge consists of the three Vedas along with their auxiliary and secondary sciences (*aṅga* and *upāṅga*). Punishment should be administered in consideration of these factors. If administered otherwise, it produces harm and does not achieve its purpose. This is a restatement for the sake of praising punishment; however, the rule for the infliction of punishment will be stated later: "Having ascertained the offense" (MDh 8.126). || 7.16 ||
That king is the personification of punishment; he is the leader and the ruler, and he is recorded as the guarantor of the dharma of the four stages of life.

The rod alone is the king, because kingship exists by virtue of it; it alone is the man, for it subdues even the most powerful men and brings them under its control like women; it is the leader, since it is out of fear of it that affairs are properly guided; it is the ruler, for it is with reference to it that the power of punishment (*vāsanā*) becomes effective as a rule; and it is the surety, acting as a guarantor against the transgression of the social classes and stages of life. (7.17)
And since this is so, therefore:
Punishment governs all subjects; punishment alone protects them.
Punishment keeps watch while others sleep; the wise know punishment to be dharma. (7.18)

Neither the treatise nor the king rules; for even when both the treatise and the king exist, it is solely out of fear of punishment that those belonging to the social classes and stages of life (varṇāśramiṇaḥ) follow the injunctions. And thus, it is punishment alone that protects others from those who commit improper acts. Even while the king’s officers are asleep, the world does not act according to its own whims, whether out of fear of this world or fear of the next world. (7.18)
When properly supported after due deliberation, he delights all his subjects;
but when applied without deliberation, he brings about destruction on every side. (7.19)

M D: We are not released by this much alone, namely, that what is held improperly does not perform its function. Just as when properly held it delights the subjects, so too when held improperly it destroys everything. 7.19.
If the king were not to tirelessly administer punishment to those deserving of it, the stronger would roast the weaker on a spit like fish. (7.20)
Not only is there the attainment of merit in the infliction of punishment, but in its non-infliction, the "law of the fish" prevails. (7.20)
A crow might eat excrement, and a dog might lick the sacrificial oblation; there would be no sense of ownership over anything, and the lower would prevail over the higher. (7.21)

All beings, including crows, dogs, and others, cannot be turned back even by the most excellent gods endowed with supernatural powers (*ṛddhimat*) without the use of force; how much less so anyone else? This is because they are bound by the words of friends, allies, and kinsmen. (7.21)
And this being so:
"The whole world is kept in check by punishment, for a pure man is hard to find;
indeed, out of fear of punishment, the entire world is fit for enjoyment. (7.22)

Maitreya said: "In this world, everyone is indeed conquered by punishment—that [punishment] by which one who follows the teaching, whose nature is pure, becomes difficult to find. Therefore, although this infliction of punishment produces suffering, it is nevertheless prescribed by the scripture; for there is no other means for the maintenance of the Dharma. || 7.22 ||
Gods, dānavas, gandharvas, rākṣasas, birds, and serpents—even they are made to serve for the enjoyment [of others] when oppressed by the rod alone. (7.23)

M.D.: Likewise, even though gods and others possess lordship (*īśvara*), they favor those worthy of favor and strike down those worthy of punishment solely out of fear of punishment. (M: Gods and others do not favor or strike down through the power of seizing or harming; rather, the gods favor them out of fear of punishment, and so on. If they did not fear punishment because of their sovereignty, they would act according to their own whims (M: they might even proceed [to act arbitrarily]). But they do not so act. Therefore, we conclude that even gods and others, despite possessing sovereignty, proceed toward favoring or striking down according to karma and not according to their own whims solely out of fear of punishment. This is a praise of punishment by means of this hyperbolic statement (M: by means of this statement, there is praise even of these [gods]).

—M: But having seen the wretchedness of the forest *pāṭala* trees, the *kuṭaja*, bold with its flowers, shone forth; then, beholding that, Pāla laughed. (The editor has added several sentences following this. 7.23.
And likewise:
"All social classes would become corrupted, all boundaries would be broken, and there would be universal upheaval in the world through the misuse of punishment. (7.24)

If punishment were not maintained according to justice, the duties based on the castes would fall into disorder; likewise, those very bridges of dharma, artha, and kāma would be destroyed. What more need be said? Who is able to praise the Blessed One, who is called Dharma, the upholder of punishment and the establisher of order, because of his manifold virtues? 7.24
Where the dark-hued, red-eyed Punisher, who destroys evil, moves about, there the subjects do not go astray, provided that the leader perceives rightly. (7.25)

M D: This form is praiseworthy and desired by men; therefore, having fashioned it as a metaphorical representation (*rūpaka*) despite its non-existence, he praises it—[M: or, desiring it, having fashioned it as a representation of existence, he remains]. Alternatively, the staff (*daṇḍa*) is of two forms: it bestows suffering and it bestows fear. Since it is praised by means of these two forms—the cause of fear through its dark color [M: and the cause of happiness through its madness], and the cause of suffering through its red-eyedness [M: -red-ness], this divine form is restated here exactly as it is, being directly perceived through the scriptures. The praise of the staff is concluded. || 7.25 ||
They say that the king who is a speaker of truth,
who acts after due deliberation, who is wise, and who is skilled in the matters of dharma, pleasure, and wealth, is the one who properly administers it.

The administrator of that punishment is by birth a Kṣatriya, endowed with the qualities of sovereignty and majesty resulting from his consecration; he is truthful and, being wise, applies the established punishment with impartiality, neither increasing it out of hatred nor diminishing it out of favoritism. Acting with circumspection in the determination of punishment, he takes into account the place and other factors; he is learned in discerning the exceptions and general rules regarding places and so forth, and he is skilled in matters of dharma, pleasure, and wealth, knowing their specific circumstances and remaining even-minded. Such a person they call the administrator of punishment. (7.26)
And such a king as this, leading [his subjects] properly, prospers through the three aims of life; but one who is self-indulgent, unjust, and base is destroyed by his very rod of punishment. (7.27)

Setting aside the unseen, he rectifies him by means of the visible; for when this leader is properly guided by the three aims of life, he causes his leader to prosper, yet he is struck down by punishment alone through defects such as desire. (7.27)

M D: For punishment is indeed a very great power, difficult to be wielded by those of undisciplined soul; for it destroys the king himself along with his kinsmen if he has strayed from righteousness. 7.28.

Those whose discipline is both innate and acquired through knowledge are those who have mastered themselves; by them this [Dharma] can be upheld. But for one who is the opposite of that and has strayed from it, punishment alone destroys him along with his kinsmen. (7.28)
Then he would afflict the fortresses, the kingdom, and the world with all its moving and unmoving beings,
as well as the sages and gods dwelling in the intermediate space.

M.D.: If one were to remain after killing the king along with his kinsmen, what would not have been gained by the rod (*daṇḍa*)? But for that [rod] by which one does not stop at this much, but destroys even fortresses and the like, and destroys even the gods and others who dwell in the intermediate space and the heavenly world—since the gods and sages live here by means of offerings, therefore, through such improper administration, when there is a disruption of the country and so forth, the gods and others are indeed destroyed by the cessation of their sacrifices, from whom nothing is given. And thus say the authors of the Purāṇas:
"Indeed, that sacrifice which proceeds in this world from among the castes and stages of life is traditionally held to be the cause of the stability of all divine beings. Thus [it was said].
He [was] without assistance, deluded, greedy, and of unrefined intellect.
Nor can he be led by right means when he is attached to sense-objects. || 7.30 ||

MD: Since punishment, when wrongly administered, destroys both the seen and the unseen [or: the innocent and the guilty], it cannot be rightly led by one who is without assistance, who is deluded, greedy, of unrefined intellect, and excessively addicted to sensual objects—one possessed of these five defects. || 7.30 ||
And he can be led by one endowed with the five qualities that are the opposite of those [previously mentioned]; for it is said, in order to demonstrate this:
"By one who is pure, true to his word, acting in accordance with the scriptures, possessing good assistants, and being wise, the rod of punishment can be rightly applied. (7.31)

By one who is pure, who has conquered the senses, who is true to his word, who—by the context—is free from greed, who follows the scriptures, who is undeluded, who has good companions and not no companions or foolish companions, who is wise, possessing the insight born of study of the treatises or innate intelligence, and who is mindful. || 7.31 ||
And being such as this, the king should conduct himself with justice within his own realm, be severe in punishment toward his enemies,
straightforward toward his friends, and endowed with patience toward the Brahmins. (7.32)

M D: Harsh punishment is prescribed for foreign kingdoms in order to demonstrate one's valor. A friend (*suhṛd*) is one who shares in both prosperity and adversity; he whose friendship is independent of any specific purpose is an affectionate friend (*snigdha*). One should not behave deceitfully toward such a person, whereas toward others one might even act with deceit depending on the circumstances. Among Brahmins, one should be endowed with forgiveness; even when restraining Brahmins who commit wrongful acts by means of punishment, one should restrain them with prior forgiveness rather than through anger or impulsiveness. (7.32)
For a king who conducts himself in this manner, even if he lives by gleaning ears of grain, his fame spreads throughout the world like a drop of oil upon the water. (7.33)

M.D.: For a king who conducts himself in this manner, even without a treasury, his royal fame spreads solely through the proper application of punishment; by means of this, he is able to bring even foreign kingdoms under his own control and to protect them. 7.33.
But for a king who acts contrary to this and has not conquered his own self,
his fame diminishes in the world like a drop of clarified butter upon water.

Therefore, for one who is the opposite of this, even his own kingdom shrinks due to a lack of virtue; how then could anything else endure? This concludes the praise of the administration of punishment. 7.34.

But why is it so? Because he possesses such qualities: "The king was created as the protector of all the social classes (*varṇa*) and stages of life (*āśrama*), each established in their respective duties, in due order. (7.35)
M D: [For the purpose of introduction. M: This is stated even though it already exists, for the purpose of expressing a further point—that nothing possesses such qualities. || 7.35 ||
Therefore, whatever must be done by one who protects his subjects together with his retinue,
all that I shall declare to you correctly and in due order.
This verse (7.36) is for the purpose of drawing the attention of the listeners [M: for the purpose of directing their minds].
Having risen in the morning, the king should attend upon the Brahmins—those who are learned and advanced in the knowledge of the three Vedas—and he should abide by their instruction. (7.37)

The term *trayī* refers to that which has three parts (*avayava*). Those who are advanced in both the text and the meaning of that [Veda] are the "elders learned in the three Vedas" (*traividyavṛddha*); he should attend upon them. Alternatively, those who study the three Vedas and are elders among the three Vedas—being advanced by both age and wisdom—and who are well-trained in *ānvīkṣikī* (logic) and *daṇḍanīti* (statecraft), are the "learned ones. Rising early in the morning, he should wait upon those wise men with an undistracted mind. Whatever they may say, he should carry it out without hesitation; for because of their supreme righteousness, they will never speak anything detrimental to the king. (7.37)
One should always serve elderly Brahmins who are pure and learned in the Vedas;
for one who constantly serves the elderly is honored even by the Rākṣasas. (7.38)

M D: One should serve these other brahmins who are advanced in learning for the sake of dharma alone. By serving those who are advanced, one is not only joined with dharma [or honored], but also becomes most trustworthy in the world. And for this reason, it is said that one is honored even by the *rakṣas* (demons). 7.38.
From them he should constantly learn discipline, even though his own self is already disciplined;
for a king whose self is disciplined never perishes. (7.39)

MD: Discipline (*vinaya*) is indeed twofold: innate and acquired. Knowledge disciplines one who is endowed with qualities such as a desire to learn (*śuśrūṣā*). Therefore, even if one’s self were disciplined by nature, one should nevertheless produce proficiency through practice. Why? Because such great effort is exerted toward the instilling of discipline once again. (7.39)
"For by lack of discipline many kings, though possessing great retinues, have perished; yet even those dwelling in the forest have obtained kingdoms through discipline. (7.40)
For the instruction in both ways is for the sake of instilling discipline and respect. (7.40)
Now he shows them:
Vena was ruined through his lack of discipline, as were King Nahuṣa, Sudās Paijavana, Sumukha, and Nimi. (7.41)
Pṛthu indeed obtained his kingdom through discipline, as did Manu;
Kubera attained mastery over wealth, and the son of Gādhi attained the status of a Brahmin.
With three verses, he demonstrates that discipline has perceptible fruits by means of examples such as Vena and others, in order to inspire interest in the adoption of discipline. 7.42.

And this being so, the king, whose discipline was firmly established, learned from those versed in the three Vedas the triple knowledge, the eternal science of government (*daṇḍanīti*), and the science of inquiry (*ānvīkṣikī*) which is the knowledge of the self; and he learned the various undertakings of trade and agriculture from the people. (7.43)

The term "should master" (*adhigacchet*) carries over from the previous context. Since the mastery of the Vedas has already been mentioned as being obtained from those learned in the three Vedas (*traividyas*), this renewed undertaking should be understood as intended for the mastery of its specific meaning while still in the stage of a religious student (*brahmacārin*). Alternatively, it may be for the purpose of mastering what was previously unmastered in the case of one who has completed his vows (*vratasnātaka*); or, it may be taught again with the desire to instruct him in the science of government (*daṇḍanīti*), serving as an illustrative example or an explanatory statement (*arthavāda*). Thus, he should master the science of government from those who know it. The word "eternal" (*śāśvatīm*) is used for the sake of praise; the science of government, like the Veda, possesses no end. Although everything based on the science of government can be learned from common worldly experience—since it is accomplished through visible means—nevertheless, the ignorant would not understand it, and even the wise might act without restraint in the infliction of punishment. Therefore, there is a fixed rule that one should abandon greed and avoid inflicting branding or banishment upon the innocent, and that such-and-such shall be the measure of his punishment. This restriction is desired because the traditional law (*smṛti*) regarding such rules serves a visible purpose. For this reason, the king must certainly study the science of government. He should also study logic (*ānvīkṣikī*) from those who know the self (*ātmavid*) and from those learned in that field. This being so, having acquired through it the knowledge of reality, he will attain the practice of inner contemplation (*adhyātma-prasaṃkhyāna*), which serves to quell the fluctuations of joy and sorrow during times of prosperity or calamity, and thus he will not neglect the administration of the kingdom. Furthermore, proficiency in wisdom, speech, and action arises from the mastery of logic; once attained, this becomes useful for scriptural injunctions and for matters such as conversing with neighboring kings and their envoys. And he should learn from the world the various undertakings of trade and industry that serve as the means for augmenting the treasury. (7.43)
M.D.: Furthermore, this king has been diligently instructed in knowledge and discipline;
he should apply himself day and night to the mastery of his senses.
For one who has conquered his senses is able to keep his subjects under control. (7.44)

MD: The conquest of the senses is the engagement of the ears and other faculties with sound and other objects in accordance with the scriptures. This has been described among the duties of the social classes (*varṇadharma*), [and while it was primarily taught there as self-restraint (*vinaya*),] it is here further instructed [as it pertains specifically to kings]. || 7.44 ||
M D: How indeed can this man be said to have conquered his senses?
For one should strive to avoid these ten calamities born of desire and those eight born of anger, which lead to such miserable ends. (7.45)

The mention of the two [types of] suffering arising from desire and anger is for the purpose of their abandonment; that is, through the abandonment of desire and anger. And it has been stated that their abandonment occurs through the conquest of the senses. Now, the relative strength and weakness of the class of vices is being described for the sake of emphasis, so that he might indeed abandon this more grievous class of vices with due care. (7.45)
But a lord of the earth who is addicted to vices born of desire is deprived of both wealth and dharma; yet one addicted to those born of anger is deprived even of his own self. (7.46)

Regarding these two groups, one who is addicted to the passions born of desire—such as drinking, gambling, singing, dancing, and playing musical instruments—is deprived of both wealth and virtue, because such engagement cannot possibly occur without conflict with wealth and virtue. But one who persists in the actions born of anger, such as slander and violence, having fallen into a state of hatred, is inevitably destroyed. (7.46)

Hunting, gambling, sleeping by day, slander, women, intoxication, the three types of performance (song, dance, and instrumental music), and idle wandering—this is the tenfold group born of desire. (7.47)

M D: "Born of desire" (*kāmaja*) means born from desire (*kāma*), that is, from longing; or it refers to a specific object of desire. And this [desire] arises for the sake of enjoying pleasure, or it arises for those devoted to desire from the pleasure of reflecting upon objects previously experienced. It is because of this that the group of ten is called "born of desire. The description of the nature of the category of calamities born of desire begins with hunting (*mṛgayā*) and so forth. "Hunting" (*yāna*) refers to the chase. "Sleeping by day" (*divāsvapna*) is the failure to engage in duties at the time when duties should be performed. "Slander" (*parivāda*), however, when directed against ministers and others, results in independent opposition; for when everyone is engaged in devouring the flesh on the king's back (backbiting), they do not properly attend to the king's affairs due to their laxity and pride. Furthermore, there is a well-known contradiction of *dharma* in slandering those who should not be slandered. "Women" and "intoxication"—these two are well known. "The triple symphony" (*tauryatrika*) consists of dance, song, and instrumental music. "Wandering about in vain" (*vṛthāṭyā*) is aimless wandering, or wandering for a purpose that is devoid of *dharma*, *artha*, and *sukha*, or one that serves only a slight purpose. This being the case, all of this exists in contradiction to the king's interests (*artha*). Therefore, the instruction that this category of calamities born of desire must be avoided is most appropriate. (7.47)
Slander, violence, malice, envy, jealousy, and the spoiling of property; harshness born of speech and of the rod—this is the eightfold group born of anger. (7.48)

Slander (*paiśuna*) is the state of being malicious (*heḍakatva*); and that is performed out of anger. The same applies to violence (*sāhasa*). That consists of the employment of a virtuous person in a base task, or the obstruction of their work without cause. Malice (*droha*) is secret killing, or the obstruction of one's livelihood while they are still alive. Envy (*īrṣyā*) is the desire to exclude another from sharing in common objects. Spite (*asūyā*) is the engagement in speech or action for the purpose of destroying the virtues of others, manifested through gestures such as the tossing of the tongue and lips and the movement of the hands. The spoiling of wealth (*arthadūṣaṇa*) consists of non-giving or seizing it away. Harshness of speech and punishment (*vāgdaṇḍapāruṣya*) has its meaning well known. Thus, the group born of anger is also eightfold. (7.48)
One should strive to conquer that greed which all poets know to be the root of both these; for both these two classes are born from it.

One who is greedy for women and the like indulges in the group of vices born of desire (*kāmajagaṇa*). And when he is thwarted therein, anger arises. Thus, this greed is said to be the root of the two groups of vices, desire and anger. The purpose of this instruction is to demonstrate that by abandoning it, both groups of vices cease to exist due to the absence of their cause. Alternatively, the unjust seizure of another’s property is committed out of greed; and one engaged in hunting, through the exhaustion of his own independence, inevitably seizes the property of others unjustly. Furthermore, one who persists in abandoning hunting will certainly strive to increase the treasury for the sake of achieving independence, and being occupied with that, he does not engage in hunting. The same should be explained regarding sleeping during the day and other such habits. In the case of dice, however, engagement in them is well known to proceed from greed. Likewise, even among those vices born of anger, such as slander and the like, it is only the greedy person who goes to ruin. But one proceeding solely out of anger may stop at a minor loss or reach a state of appeasement. Because greed is the common cause for one who indulges in both groups of vices, greed is said to be the root of both these groups of vices. Since the literal meaning [of greed as a root] is impossible in the other case, it follows by implication that this is an extreme censure here; it is for the sake of encouraging its abandonment, so that the success of the system of governance (*rājyatantra*) may be achieved. (7.49)
Drinking, dice, women, and hunting—in this sequence, one should know that this group of four is even more grievous within the set born of desire. (7.50)

It is well known that this group of four—beginning with sleeping during the day—is more difficult [to overcome] and possesses many faults; thus, this [verse] should be explained on the basis of that renown. 7.50.
One should always know that this triad—the infliction of punishment, verbal abuse, and the embezzlement of wealth—is most grievous even within the group born of anger. (7.51)
This group of three is also well known to be more wicked than those such as the slanderers; it is renowned as being of evil birth. || 7.51 ||
A self-possessed person should know that among this group of seven vices which are everywhere interconnected, each preceding one is more grievous than the next. (7.52)

M D: Between drinking and gambling, drinking is more serious. For in that case there is the loss of consciousness, the madness of one who is not mad, the state of being a ghost for one who is not dead, the abandonment of learning and wisdom, the loss of friends, separation from the virtuous, association with the wicked, addiction to singing and other pursuits that destroy wealth, and the disclosure of secret counsel through the force of intoxication—these are the faults of drinking. In gambling, however, even for one skilled in dice, what is won is merely a gain, while for one ignorant of the game, defeat is certain. Between the vices of gambling and women, gambling is more serious. Through it, even the very wealth won becomes the prey of others, and likewise, it leads to a continuous chain of enmity. Victory is common to both sides, but defeat results in the destruction of one's followers. Furthermore, by suppressing the urges of urine and excrement, there is a weakening of the body’s constitution and the onset of disease; through indulgence, there is excessive suffering from hunger and other such afflictions. Even when his mother has died, the gambler continues to play; and when questioned during times of distress, he even becomes angry at his friends—these are the faults of gambling. In the vice of women, however, there is the procreation of offspring, the maintenance of personal grooming and abundant food, and the constant pursuit of religious merit and wealth. Moreover, a woman can be employed for the king’s welfare or used to distract an enemy. Between the vices of women and hunting, the vice of women is more serious. It leads to the neglect of duties, a sense of indifference toward royal affairs due to attachment to the company of women, the wasting of time, the loss of dharma, and a connection to the faults of drinking. Furthermore, it involves addiction to dancing and other pursuits that destroy wealth. In hunting, however, there is physical exercise, the reduction of bile, phlegm, fat, and sweat, proficiency in hitting targets whether moving or stationary, the development of skill in weaponry, and the gaining of experience with the common folk. Thus, among the fourfold group arising from desire, each preceding one is more evil than the next. Therefore, one should diligently avoid each preceding one of them. Regarding the threefold group arising from anger, between physical assault and verbal abuse, physical assault is more serious. For when the body is destroyed, it cannot be restored; whereas in the case of verbal abuse, the fire of anger born of resentment cannot be extinguished by the waters of gifts and honors. Between verbal abuse and the disparagement of wealth, verbal abuse is more serious. For those possessed of spirit do not find a remedy for the agitation of their minds caused by harsh words. And thus runs the proverb:
Having pierced through firm, well-aimed, and deeply embedded bone,
words do not extract the splinter from the limbs, nor even from the heart.
A forest pierced by arrows or struck down by an axe grows back;
but a wound inflicted by harsh, loathsome speech does not heal.

[**Verses also found in Medhātithi’s commentary on MDh 7.52**: Having pierced a firm, well-aimed arrow that has entered the bone, physicians extract the shaft and leave the limb free of the barb; yet words do not even depart from the heart. A forest pierced by arrows grows back, and one struck by an axe regrows; but the wound caused by speech does not heal, for a loathsome word spoken is never forgotten.]

Since wealth depends upon fortune, those possessed of splendor do not take account of the impairment of that wealth. In this very same way, it has been explained that among these three things born of anger, each preceding one is more grievous than the next. (7.52)
Between calamity and death, calamity is said to be the more grievous;
for one who suffers calamity goes downward, while one who dies without calamity goes to heaven. (7.53)

This censure of vices is stated in general terms for the purpose of avoiding them. Although death is all-devouring (*sarvahara*) among vices, nevertheless, there is this distinction between the two: death is all-devouring in this world alone, whereas vice is so in both worlds. Alternatively, the meaning of this verse should be stated exactly as it is heard. By speaking thus, a prohibition is expressed regarding those human qualities born of desire and anger when they have become vices, but not regarding their slight indulgence. For when these are practiced habitually, having become vices, they destroy virtue, wealth, and life, and cause the laxity of the administration of the kingdom. Furthermore, even excessive indulgence has been mentioned, as in the statement that it is "impossible for a king" (or "not possible for a king"). Therefore, there is a prohibition of these things called vices. Thus, for the sake of a king free from vice attaining the excellence of virtuous allies, the characteristics of ministers are now described. (7.53)
He should appoint seven or eight ministers who are hereditary, learned in the treatises, brave, skilled in hitting the mark, of noble birth, and thoroughly tested.

[Mūlam]: [Ancestral lineage], those descended from that lineage, and the hereditary local people. By the mention of "learned in the sciences" (*śāstravid*), all the qualities of a minister are included by implication. These are as follows: wise, of noble form, retentive, dexterous, eloquent, bold, resolute, endowed with energy and majesty, enduring of hardship, pure, friendly, possessed of the power of virtue and noble fortitude, free from arrogance and fickleness, beloved, and one who does not create enmities—this is the excellence of a minister. By the word "heroic" (*śūra*), one who is indifferent even toward body, wife, children, and wealth for the sake of the king's business is understood; or else, its meaning is simply according to common usage. By the mention of "one who has attained his mark" (*labdhalakṣa*), one who has observed and practiced those specific duties is meant. For those born of noble family generally do not engage in improper acts. The word *saciva* is a synonym for "companion. The mention of "seven or eight" is for the sake of restriction; because if there are too few, there is the defect of a lack of unanimity, and if there are too many, there is the leakage of counsel and the division of factions. "Well-tested" means tested by the trials of virtue, wealth, pleasure, and fear. This testing is described as follows: A domestic priest (*purohita*), having been dismissed under a pretext by the king for some minor matter and being unable to endure it, should secretly instigate each minister individually, saying: "This king is unrighteous. Therefore, it would be well if we were to install a righteous person—one of noble birth, already in favor, uniquely distinguished, a neighboring king, or a forest chieftain. And this is pleasing to the other ministers; what do you think? If he refuses, he is proven pure by the trial of virtue. A commander-in-chief (*senāpati*), having been dismissed by the king for accepting improper gifts, should, in the presence of all, instigate each minister individually through trusted men with the distribution of much wealth for the purpose of destroying the king, saying: "This is pleasing to all the ministers; what do you think? If he refuses, he is proven pure by the trial of wealth. A female ascetic who has gained confidence within the harem should instigate each minister individually, saying: "The queen desires you, and she has devised a means for a meeting with you. [If he refuses, he is proven pure by the trial of pleasure. Certain men employed by the king should spread a rumor: "The king is to be killed by the ministers who have made a pact. When the rumor has been heard among the ministers, a trusted agent of the domestic priest should leak the secret counsel among the ministers, saying: "Having overheard this rumor, the king has resolved to suppress you. Then, one of those very men who has made a prior agreement should incite them individually against the royal ministers. Among them, those who refuse are proven pure by the trial of fear.

Alternatively, he should first appoint as collectors of revenue (*arthasamāhartṛ*), treasurers (*saṃnidhātṛ*), and administrators of financial affairs (*arthavyavahārin*) those who are hereditary. He should appoint as wise counselors (*prajñāsaciva*) those learned in the *śāstras*. He should appoint as enforcers of extraordinary punishments (*daṇḍātiśayavyavahārin*) those who are brave. The meaning of "all these" is that they must be experienced (*labdhalakṣa*), having been tested for their integrity, loyalty, and capability. The phrase "of noble birth" (*kulodgata*) is a qualification applying to all of them previously. He should appoint seven or eight ministers, as the case may require, after carefully considering the royal duties. The phrase "well-tested" (*suparīkṣita*) is a qualification for all ministers. How so? It means they have been proven pure through all the secret tests (*sarvopadhā*) by means of spies. This testing applies to matters other than those concerning the king himself, but not in the manner described before; otherwise, this very point would be the reason for the distinction in their purity. Regarding the proficiency of the ministers, ministers are appointed by the king for various tasks and purposes. (7.54)
M D: Because even an action that is easy to perform is difficult for one person alone;
how much more so a kingdom of great consequence when undertaken without assistance? (7.55)

And this being so, since there is no prescription for [a fixed number of] ministers, there may be only one minister for the king as circumstances permit. And having done so, it has been stated: "Thus [it is said] regarding the best of kings. (7.55) In that regard, he should constantly deliberate on matters common to both peace and war together with those who are his ministers and counselors.
The place, the origin, the protection, and the methods for calming what has been acquired. || 7.56 ||

With them, he should deliberate upon the sixfold policy (*ṣāḍguṇya*), such as making peace or war, examining common merits and defects, strengths and weaknesses. He should not keep this entirely secret; however, that which is the determination of what must be done—the supreme secret—he should decide by himself alone with his own mind. In this way, this king does not become subject to the influence of others. Furthermore, as for the other point—"he should deliberate on the *sthānas* (bases of power) together with them"—that consists of four kinds: the army (*daṇḍa*), the treasury (*kośa*), the city (*pura*), and the kingdom (*rāṣṭra*). Among these, the army consists of elephants, horses, chariots, and infantry. One must deliberate on their training, maintenance, protection, and so forth. Likewise, regarding the treasury, one must deliberate on the abundance of gold and silver, as well as income, expenditure, and security. Similarly, regarding the kingdom—which is the territory and its revenue—one must deliberate on whether it provides a livelihood for oneself and sustains others; whether it is easy to protect in times of calamity and not difficult to guard; whether it is suitable for cattle, free from enemies and pests, rich in arable land (*sītā*), and possesses protected pastures; whether it abounds in livestock, is not dependent on rain (*adevamātṛka*), and can withstand the burden of taxes and military force in times of distress, and so forth. Regarding the city, he will state later: "It should be well-supplied with weapons," and so on.

Alternatively, *sthāna* (the state) is non-deprivation from one’s own territory. In this way, the *samudayas* (sources of revenue) are to be considered. These include agriculture, cattle-rearing, plantations, trade routes, customs duties, fines, and so forth. He will explain later the protection (*gupti*) pertaining to one’s own kingdom. The pacification of what has been acquired consists of: providing gifts and honors to deities, hermitages, the learned, the righteous, and the brave; granting permission to those who are accustomed [to their duties]; the release of all prisoners; favoring the poor, the helpless, and the sick; initiating new festivals and continuing those already established. Furthermore, having removed any conduct that harms the treasury or the army, or that is unrighteous, he should establish righteous administration. As it is said: "One should cause to be practiced righteous conduct not yet performed, and that which has been performed by others; one should not cause unrighteous conduct to be practiced, nor should one allow that which has been performed by others to continue. In this manner, the states and other matters are to be considered. 7.56.
Having ascertained each of their individual intentions, he should act for his own benefit by engaging them separately in their respective tasks. (7.57)

One who wishes to acquire wisdom from others should question those ministers both individually and collectively. For there may be some person who is lacking in presence of mind in an assembly, yet is bold in private; or one whose intellect falters in an assembly, though it was unimpeded elsewhere. Therefore, he should question them in both ways. He should then determine what they have said, whether it was taught by one among them or another, provided it is not contradicted and is free from fault. (7.57)
But the king should deliberate on the supreme counsel concerning the sixfold policy with a distinguished, wise Brahmin among all his ministers.
For the Brahmin, being more highly wise and righteous, is trustworthy because of his faultlessness. (7.58)
This being the case, one who has constant confidence in him should entrust all affairs to him;
having reached a decision together with him, one should then carry out the work. (7.59)
He should also appoint other ministers who are pure, wise, steadfast, thoroughly tested, and capable of properly collecting revenue.

The King should appoint these men, endowed with the qualities of ministers, after they have been thoroughly tested through all types of secret trials (*upadhā*). This rule regarding the fixed number—whether seven or eight—is stated as an exception for those who are assistants to the King, such as the collectors of revenue and the treasurers. (7.60)
He should appoint as many diligent, capable, and discerning men as are required for his duties. (7.61)

MD: The collection of these ministers of the king should be according to the magnitude of their duties. For the reason that, due to the engagement in tasks, someone might fall into despondency through some other lack of application; and even one who is capable may become negligent because of such negligence. (7.61)
For their sake, he should appoint those who are brave, capable, and of noble birth to the management of mines and works;
and those who are pure and timid to the duties within the inner apartments.

For their sake, pure men who are experts in the income and expenditure of wealth should be appointed as treasury officers. Those who have proven their mettle in action and are undaunted should be made commanders of the army; however, those who are timid should be assigned to duties such as food distribution. All of these should be made capable, for they, disregarding the onset of adversities through their habit of perseverance, do not let the time for their master’s business pass by. (7.62)
And he should appoint as his messenger one who is learned in all the scriptures, who understands gestures, facial expressions, and conduct, and who is pure, skillful, and of noble birth. (7.63)

An envoy should be endowed with the full complement of ministerial qualities, according to the instruction that he must be proficient in all treatises (*śāstra*). Furthermore, these gestures (*iṅgita*), facial expressions (*ākāra*), and physical movements (*ceṣṭā*) must necessarily be understood by the envoy regarding the king in a foreign territory. In that context, when the king desires to make peace, the envoy’s attentive reception, his inspired confidence, his frequent and gentle honors, and his appreciation of the king’s words without malice—these are the signs. Conversely, the opposite of these indicates a desire to seize [the territory]. As for facial expression (*ākāra*): it pertains to the body; a withered face, a change in complexion, silence, long and hot sighs, and other such bodily distortions indicate dejection. A bright face, eloquence in speech, and grooming of the body, and so forth, indicate joy. Regarding physical movements (*ceṣṭā*): failing to rise to meet [the envoy] during activities reveals dejection accompanied by despair over the failure of the mission; conversely, rising to meet him indicates joy in the opposite case. Purity in this envoy must concern both women and wealth; this is specifically taught. For in connection with women there is the disclosure of secret counsel (*mantra-bheda*), and in the seizure of wealth there is humiliation and the ruin of the task. Thus, the purpose of one born of noble lineage has been stated. (7.63)
Maitreya said: For what reason, then, is this definition of an envoy stated with such care?
Because: "One who is devoted, pure, skillful, mindful, and knowledgeable of place and time; who is handsome, fearless, eloquent—such an envoy is praised by kings. (7.64)

M D: He is loyal and cannot be led astray; he is pure and remains unswayed in matters concerning women. He is skillful and does not transgress the bounds of place and time. Being mindful, he delivers his master’s message without losing its intent through forgetfulness. Knowing the proper place and time, he accomplishes every task. Possessing a fine physique, he is invincible; and because he is pleasant to behold, his words are accepted. Free from fear, he reports his master’s message exactly as it was, even if it is harsh. He does so repeatedly. Being eloquent, he is capable of providing replies and counter-arguments to the message. || 7.64 ||

M D: For what purpose is this instruction on the characteristics and duties of an envoy given? [It is because: "The army depends upon the minister; the administration of justice depends upon the army; the treasury and the realm depend upon the king; but peace and its opposite depend upon the envoy. (7.65)

Just as the army consisting of elephants, horses, and so forth is dependent upon the commander-in-chief—since the application of punishment in royal affairs proceeds according to his will—and just as the kingdom prospers through the king’s energetic efforts and intended purpose, but declines through neglect; even so, peace and war are dependent upon the envoy. This is a praise of the envoy based on the connection with these actual facts, for this is precisely the view held [by the author]. (7.65)
For it is the messenger indeed who unites those who are divided and divides those who are united;
the messenger performs that action by which men are alienated. (7.66)
For it is said that by means of both the differentiation and the concealment of the mantra, this [mantra] performs both [functions], namely the movement and the fear of the messenger. 7.66.

He should discern, through secret gestures and movements, the king's facial expression, his intentions, and his conduct regarding his servants, his officials, and his enemies—specifically, what they intend to do. (7.67)

M [D omits this commentary]: He should know the king's intention—that is, his purpose regarding his duties and affairs—through his own concealed gestures and movements, namely the facial expressions, hints, and physical postures intended for those royal tasks he wishes to perform.
And having understood in truth everything intended by the enemy king—
whether it be good or bad— as well as the efforts of his circle of servants, he should apply himself in such a way that he does not bring suffering upon himself. (7.68)

M D: A messenger should carry out peace, war, and other diplomatic actions without causing distress to his master. Likewise, he should enter the capital only when permitted. He should establish alliances with forest-dwellers and frontier guards. He should observe the terrain suitable for obstructing battle. He should ascertain the dimensions of forts and the countryside, as well as their strategic strength. Even at the risk to his own life, he should deliver the message exactly as stated. He should not be arrogant because of the honors shown him. He should endure unpleasant speech. He should avoid intoxication. He should win over those who are susceptible to intrigue. He should know the degree of loyalty and disloyalty among the subjects of the enemy king. He should not disclose the size of his own forces under any pretext, such as a claim of ignorance or distraction. Furthermore, he should carry out all other tasks that assist the enemy's undertaking, including the seizure of relatives and jewels, and the provision of secret intelligence. (7.68)

One should dwell in a country that is arid yet rich in crops, predominantly inhabited by noble people, free from turmoil, delightful, with submissive vassals, and providing a means of livelihood. (7.69)

One should dwell in a country that is *jāṅgala*—characterized by various kinds of grains, roots, fruits, flowers, grass, and fuel; abundant in crops and free from famine; inhabited mostly by noble people and filled with Brāhmaṇas for the sake of protecting the Dharma and other virtues; untroubled and not disturbed by wild beasts, reptiles, thieves, gadflies, mosquitoes, and the like; delightful with groves and trees flourishing with blossoms in all seasons; where neighboring vassals are submissive and bowed down; providing a livelihood through clear-watered reservoirs; and adorned with rows of very spacious houses and palaces. One should settle in a land endowed with these qualities of a *jāṅgala* region and other such regional excellences. (7.69)
Having taken refuge in a desert fortress, an earth fortress, a water fortress, or even a forest fortress, or a human fortress, or a mountain fortress, one should dwell there as a city.

A desert fort (*dhanvadurga*) is an area extending for five *yojanas* in every direction that is devoid of water, lacking trees, shrubs, or the shade of creepers, and contains abundant underground water; it is such that it cannot be reached by an enemy. A mountain fort (*mahīdurga*) is surrounded by a wall made of brick or stone, twice as high as its width, rising more than twelve cubits, with a base like a palm tree and a top adorned with battlements (*kapiśīrṣaka*), and provided with a solid rampart. A water fort (*abdurga*) is encircled by deep water that cannot be drained. A forest fort (*vārkṣadurga*) is covered on all sides for half a *yojana* with dense, large trees. A human fort (*nṛdurga*) is occupied by a fourfold army and consists mostly of men skilled in excellent weaponry. A hill fort (*giridurga*) is a mountain ridge that is difficult to climb, accessible by only a single path, and supplied with water from rivers and springs. (7.70)
But with every effort, one should take refuge in a mountain fortress;
for by virtue of its many advantages, the mountain fortress is distinguished above all others.
M D: Among these types of fortresses, the mountain fortress is the best because it is the most invulnerable. 7.71.
Of these, the first three are inhabited by wild beasts, cave-dwellers, and water-frequenters; the latter three are inhabited, respectively, by monkeys, humans, and gods. (7.72)
Just as enemies do not harm those who have taken refuge in a fortress, so too do foes not injure a king who has sought shelter in a stronghold. (7.73)
M D: These two verses of scriptural authority are for the purpose of ensuring respectful practice. 7.72–73.
A single archer standing upon a rampart can fight a hundred; a hundred can fight ten thousand. Therefore, a fortress is constructed. (7.74)

M D: This demonstrates that a mountain fort has the quality of being directly perceptible [or: possesses direct visibility]. And thus, the specific advantage of each respective type of fort should be understood. 7.74.
That [city] shall be well-provided with weapons, wealth, grain, and vehicles;
with brahmins, artisans, machines, fodder, and water. (7.75)

This verse is intended to demonstrate those who possess the necessary purpose and timing for besieging a fortress. This being the case, whatever other purposes and timings are relevant—such as those concerning surgery, toxicology, medicine, and astrology—those too should be understood as included. (7.75)
In its center, he should have his own house constructed,
spacious, well-protected, pleasant in all seasons, bright, and provided with water and trees.
He should have a house built according to his own means, spacious, with rooms suited to the seasons, and provided with underground tunnels and other such features. (7.76)
Having occupied that [seat], he should marry a wife of the same caste who possesses auspicious marks, born of a noble family, pleasing, and endowed with beauty and virtue. (7.77)

M.D.: This is a restatement of those [sons] previously mentioned—such as the *savarṇa* and others—with reference to their connection to being taken from a noble family for the purpose of assisting in the administration of the kingdom. (7.77)
He should appoint a domestic priest and choose officiating priests; they shall perform for him the domestic rites as well as those pertaining to the sacrificial fires. (7.78)

The domestic priest (purohita) should be endowed with the qualities of a minister as well as the qualities of a Brahmin; the officiating priests (ṛtvij), however, need only be endowed with the qualities of a Brahmin. (7.78)
The king should sacrifice with various rituals accompanied by abundant sacrificial fees; and for the sake of dharma, he should bestow enjoyments and wealth upon the brahmins. (7.79)
M.D.: These two—sacrifice and giving—are prescribed for the king as superior duties. Just like the obligatory rites, there is indeed sin in the non-performance of these two as well. (7.79)
He should cause the annual tribute to be collected from the kingdom by trusted agents;
he should be devoted to the sacred tradition in this world and behave toward men like a father.

From the sources of revenue as previously described, he should collect tribute according to the authority of the sacred tradition by taking one-sixth or one-eighth of the produce and so forth. He should behave toward those who pay taxes and others like a father—[as the commentary notes: "like a father" means he should be impartial toward friend and foe]. He should appoint various learned supervisors in their respective places;
they shall oversee all the legal affairs of men as they carry them out. (7.81)

The king should appoint various learned officials as superintendents over the gold treasury, merchandise, raw materials, weapons, weights, tolls, ships, elephants, horses, chariots, and infantry. All of these should be understood as being endowed with the full qualities of a minister. 7.81.
He should be a worshiper of those brahmins who have returned from the teacher’s house;
for this inexhaustible treasure of the brahmins is ordained for kings. (7.82)

This gift of a restrictive obligation (*niyamadāna*) is also prescribed for the king to bestow upon those who have completed their studentship (*snātaka*). For there is sin for one who does not give even to these; and so it has been said: "One who is unwilling to give deserves abandonment" (MDh 10.113). || 7.82 ||
Neither thieves nor enemies carry it off, nor does it perish;
therefore, the king should deposit this inexhaustible treasure with the brahmins. (7.83)

Just as there is no destruction of a treasure by thieves, forest-dwellers, enemies, or those who seize the king’s property in the same way that occurs through the giving of gold and other goods to Brahmins and others—this is an explanatory praise (*arthavāda*) intended to extol the necessity of making such gifts. (7.84)
And this is another [verse]: "What is offered into the mouth of a Brahmin never overflows, it does not cause distress, and it is never lost; it is superior to the Agnihotra sacrifices. (7.84)

Just as a poured oblation that spills is defective due to the breaking of the vessel, and just as an oblation is lost when the deity is not recognized, so too is there a Brāhmaṇa passage stating: "This oblation which is offered without having recognized the deity is indeed half-offered. This being the case, the censure regarding the three defects of the oblation is intended as a praise for the gift prescribed in the current Brāhmaṇa passage. Thus it has been said: "It is superior to the Agnihotra offerings," meaning superior to the Agnihotra and other such rites. This should be understood in this way as including all obligatory duties (*nityakarman*). Some say that because of the mention of the "mouth," this refers specifically to the giving of food; however, that is incorrect. Because of the scriptural statement, "The twice-born is declared to have his hands as his mouth" (MDh 4.117), this should be understood as referring to the subject of all forms of acceptance (*pratigraha*). 7.84.
And this is another point:

A gift given to a non-Brahmin yields an equal reward; to one who merely calls himself a Brahmin, it yields a twofold reward; to a teacher, it yields a thousandfold reward; but to one who has mastered the Vedas, it yields an infinite reward. (7.85)

And for this reason, gifts should be given to these [latter]. Since this section concerns the praise of the restrictive giving to virtuous *snātaka* Brahmins, the mention of non-Brahmins and others should be understood as being for the purpose of praising the gift to the learned. How so? It would not be appropriate [to give] to a non-Brahmin or one who merely calls himself a Brahmin; [rather, even when given to those two, the gift bears fruit—how much more so to those possessed of noble lineage, refinement, study, wisdom, conduct, and ritual action]. Furthermore, this restrictive giving (*niyatadāna*) is the subject under discussion, and that is not possible in the case of a non-Brahmin or one who merely calls himself a Brahmin.
And it is said:

"One should honor with offerings to the gods and ancestors those learned in the Vedas (*śrotriya*) who have completed their studies and vows and have come to one's house; but one should avoid those who are the opposite. (MDh 4.31)

And this is not an injunction regarding the fruit; for if it were an injunction regarding the fruit, it would apply to the giving of gifts for the sake of desired results (*kāmyadāna*). Thus, by the force of the meaning as stated, this is not an injunction regarding the fruit; rather, this verse is intended to provide instruction on the ritual procedure (*kalpa*). Otherwise, the context would be interrupted. Alternatively, since the giving to non-Brāhmaṇas and others occurs when the aforementioned causes—such as those involving the distressed and the helpless—are present, this may be a specific duty (*viśeṣadharma*) of kings, intended to demonstrate the distinction in the fruit resulting from the excellence of the recipient (*pātra*). For praise is never bestowed without cause. (7.85)
And so says the following verse:
"Indeed, according to the excellence of the recipient and through faith alone, one obtains the fruit of a gift—whether small or great—after death. (7.86)

M.D.: This being the case, just as there is a distinction in the fruit according to the distinction of the recipient (*pātra*), so too—in the case of giving to Brāhmaṇas who are equal—this [statement] must be understood as an exception to the rule regarding the distinction of the recipient. Now, this explanation is provided for the second half of the preceding verse. Furthermore, it is not logical that the gift-object (*deyadravya*) be equal to the fruit either by way of genus (*jāti*) or by way of quantity (*parimāṇa*), because that would contradict both scripture (*śāstra*) and logic (*nyāya*). How, then, is this [verse] to be explained as "equal"? According to worldly convention (*lokaprasiddhi*), it is neither superior nor inferior; that which is neither is "equal. Thus, taking what is commonly known in the world as the limit, the doubling and so forth of the fruit should be stated. Others, however, think that a fruit equal to the gift-object is not possible; therefore, the equality should be understood as residing in the giver. Having given even alms-food (*bhikṣā*) to one who is not a Brāhmaṇa, one obtains the enjoyment of the fruit of that gift through a human body alone, but not from giving to a superior recipient (*pātra*). This point requires investigation. Moreover, those who are "non-Brāhmaṇas" (*abrāhmaṇa*) are the Kṣatriyas and Vaiśyas. And thus it is stated in Gautama’s section on the giving of alms: "The two immediately following the Brāhmaṇa caste [are the Kṣatriya and Vaiśya]. Furthermore, the usage [is seen in]: "Acquisition of knowledge from a non-Brāhmaṇa" (GDh 7.1). There is no acquisition of knowledge from a Śūdra who is a non-Brāhmaṇa, due to the greed for wealth and because of scriptural prohibitions. [The phrase] "from one who is not a Brāhmaṇa" refers to one who is not of the Brāhmaṇa caste, because of the absolute superiority of the Brāhmaṇa birth, and because [the rule applies] "not to one who is unequal or uninitiated. However, in the case of Kṣatriyas and Vaiśyas who are religious students (*brahmacārin*), the acceptance of alms and so forth is indeed permitted, by virtue of the authority of the instruction [regarding such acceptance]. Thus, in this sense, it is more appropriate to understand that even those two are included by the word "non-Brāhmaṇa. (7.86)
When summoned by those who are equal, superior, or inferior while protecting his subjects, the king, mindful of the duty of a Kṣatriya, must not retreat from battle. (7.87)
M D: When summoned by anyone—even by one superior in strength—there should be no retreat from battle; for this is indeed the distinguished duty of kings. (7.87)
Not retreating in battles, the protection of subjects, and service toward the Brahmins— this is the supreme means for the welfare of kings. (7.88)
Just as protecting the subjects and serving the Brahmins are the preeminent duties of kings, so too is not retreating in battles; this is the praise of non-retreat (anivṛtti). || 7.88 ||
And so it is said: "In battles, kings who desire to slay one another, fighting with their utmost strength and not turning their backs, go to heaven. (7.89)
And therefore, not retreating from battle is the specific duty of kings; and for one fighting, a rule is prescribed. (7.89)
While fighting his enemies in battle, he should not strike them with deceptive weapons, nor with barbed ones, nor with those that are burnt, nor with those whose points are blazing with fire. (7.90)
One should not strike one who has ascended to dry land, nor a eunuch, nor one with palms joined in supplication;
nor one with disheveled hair, nor one who is seated, nor one who says, "I am yours. (7.91)

One should not strike one who is asleep, nor one who is unarmored, nor one who is naked, nor one who is unarmed, nor one who is not fighting, nor one who is looking on, nor one who has already encountered another opponent. (7.92)

Recalling the dharma of the virtuous, he did not strike one who was suffering from a weapon-wound, nor one who was distressed, nor one who had not been thoroughly tested, nor one who was terrified, nor one who had turned his back in flight. (7.93)
M: The rule regarding the regulations for battle is intended to prevent sin incurred by acting otherwise than this.
D: This rule regarding the regulations for battle is for the purpose of preventing the sin of killing them. 7.90–93.
But he who, being afraid, turns his back in battle and is slain by enemies, incurs all whatever evil deed his master has committed. (7.94)
And whatever merit he has acquired for the sake of the next world—[or here], his master takes all of that from him when he is slain after turning back. (7.95)

M D: For both the king and the other man—the executioner—turning back is censured in two verses, and that censure is appropriate; for by failing to do that for which he was brought along, he indeed incurs sin. (7.94–95)
Chariots, horses, elephants, umbrellas, wealth, grain, livestock, women,
all types of goods, and base metals— whatever anyone conquers belongs to him.
M.D.: This restriction is for the purpose of precluding the inclusion of the king [as a recipient], because he is the master. 7.96.
"But one should give a special share to the king; such is the Vedic revelation.
And the king must give to all the warriors that which has been won in common. (7.97)

M.D.: The king shall take the *uddhāra* (extra share) and the surplus wealth from all the warriors. There is a Vedic revelation (*śruti*) stating, "Having slain Vṛtra, he took Mahendra as his *uddhāra*," and so forth. Regarding that which was won not individually but by the collective force, and likewise that which was honored by the king, a portion corresponding to the hardship of the exertion in battle must be given to all the warriors. (7.97)
This eternal law of warriors has been declared as unadorned; a Kṣatriya, slaying his enemies in battle, should not deviate from this dharma. (7.98)

"Unadorned" (anupaskṛta) means uncreated, having qualities established by its own nature; that is to say, not produced by effort and free from defects. That which is defective is adorned for the purpose of instilling qualities. This is a verse of summary. || 7.98 ||
One should seek to obtain what has not been obtained, guard with effort what has been obtained, increase what has been guarded, and bestow what has been increased upon worthy recipients. (7.99)

A king who desires to obtain [wealth], though striving for it, may be destroyed by his rivals—his great kinsmen who are ever-increasing—because his administration is weak. Even if he protects what has been acquired, he is diminished by the mere toil of acquisition, which yields no fruit. And if he does not properly increase what he has protected, it perishes. One who consumes it himself, having no one else to share it with, fails to bestow upon worthy recipients that which was acquired, protected, and increased through three great efforts; thus he is deprived of the next world. Through his lack of desire, he incurs the threefold affliction that is the result of those three efforts. (7.99)
One should know that this fourfold [dharma] is the means for achieving the goals of human life;
one should perform its constant practice correctly and without sloth. (7.100)

One should seek what is not yet obtained by means of force; one should protect what has been obtained with vigilance; one should increase what has been protected through growth; and one should bestow what has been increased upon worthy recipients. (7.101)

M D: Here, by the word "interest" (*vṛddhi*), the means for the sake of interest is expressed, due to the force of the context. One should deposit the increased amount into worthy recipients through the giving of interest. [The fourfold] instruction [M: the instruction on the means] is for the sake of accomplishing the king's human goals. 7.100–01.
M D: Since this is so, therefore:

He should always have his rod of punishment raised; he should always display his manly prowess; he should always keep his movements concealed; and he should always seek out the enemy's vulnerabilities. (7.102)

The king should constantly train his forces—elephants and the rest—in riding and other skills, and he should maintain his weapons and armor in good condition. By doing so, his state of being one whose rod of punishment is ever-raised becomes manifest throughout the royal circle. At border posts, forest outposts, and other strategic locations, men who are trustworthy, armored, and clad in mail must remain perpetually on guard. In this way, his state of having displayed valor becomes evident. He should protect and win over those on the side of potential traitors, while remaining concealed in his own movements and pursuing the vulnerabilities of his enemies. (7.102)
The entire world trembles before one who constantly holds up the rod of punishment;
therefore, he should subdue all beings by means of that very rod. (7.103)
For one who has raised the rod of punishment, the submission of enemies occurs without effort; [M: the destruction of the enemy faction—this is the praise of the rod. || 7.103 ||
One should always conduct oneself without guile and never with guile; being ever well-restrained, one should recognize the guile employed by an enemy.

A king should not, at the outset, instigate seditious intrigue (*upajāpa*) against the subjects of another king who are angry, greedy, fearful, or proud. However, regarding those within his own realm or even those in the realm of an enemy who have acted righteously, he may later employ intrigue against them through his intelligence; because of his righteousness, universal affection is easily won. In this regard, the group of the "angry" (*kruddhavarga*) consists of those who have been deceived, those who have been insulted despite performing equal service in craft or assistance, those whose favorites have been superseded, those whose kinsmen have been exiled, those prevented from practicing false conduct, those excluded by their own relatives, and those whose entire property has been confiscated. The group of the "fearful" (*bhītavarga*) consists of those who commit evil deeds, those who are distressed by punishments for equal offenses, those from adjacent territories, those who have submitted to force, those stationed in all administrative offices, and those who have suddenly accumulated wealth. The group of the "greedy" (*lubdhavarga*) consists of those who are impoverished, miserly, addicted to vices, and so forth. The group of the "proud" (*mānivarga*) consists of those who are self-conceited, those who resent the honor shown to enemies, those humiliated by inferiors, the fierce, the reckless, and those dissatisfied with their enjoyments. Having identified these among both the enemy and his own side, the king should protect himself and instigate intrigue against them. (7.104)
An enemy should not know one's own vulnerability, but one should know the vulnerability of the enemy;
