like a tortoise, one should withdraw one's limbs and guard one's own weak points. (7.105)

M.D.: Through excessive application, it is possible to conceal one's own vulnerabilities and observe the vulnerabilities of others. One should learn of these through the deployment of secret agents (*gūḍhapuruṣa*), such as fraudulent spies (*kāpaṭika*) and others, within one’s own territory, and likewise within the territory of the enemy. (7.105)
One should deliberate on matters like a crane, dart away like a hare, snatch like a wolf, and display prowess like a lion. (7.106)
M: has transposed pāda b and d.

M D: Just as a crane, by means of constant attendance, discovers through meditative application (*dhyāna-yoga*) the means to capture a school of fish residing in a fortress-like lake due to their own nature, so too one should not fall into despondency, thinking that even objectives extremely difficult to attain are reached through excessive application to the contemplation of goals. Just as a hare, because of its small body, is able to escape even from a host of enemies, so too one who is alone and without allies, unable to remain when provoked on all sides by neighboring kings, should seek refuge with a virtuous person after securing a fortress and escaping from that situation. And just as a wolf, intent on seizing livestock, seizes them upon finding the negligence of the herdsman, so too one should not abandon the effort to seize [the enemy's] wealth, thinking oneself solely intent on self-protection; for there will come a time when, like the wolf, one shall seize [the prize]. And just as a lion, through the application of the power of valor, slays even large-bodied elephants and other animals by attacking them, so too one should not be deterred by the thought that the enemy force is great; for even that which is large may be slain by a small being possessing great vital strength (*mahā-prāṇa*). 7.106.
Thus, while he is victorious, whatever adversaries he may have,
he should bring them all under his control through the expedients beginning with conciliation.
When a king is thus established in victory, those who do not submit to his majesty he should subsequently bring under his control through conciliation and other such means. (7.107)
If, however, they do not abide by the first three expedients, one should gradually bring them under control by force with the rod. 7.108.
M: Because of the rule regarding the application of force (*daṇḍa*) as the last of the means beginning with conciliation (*sāma*). D:
When the three means beginning with conciliation have been exhausted, there is the rule for the application of force. 7.108.
Regarding the four means of policy beginning with conciliation, the wise always praise both conciliation and force for the constant prosperity of the kingdom. (7.109)

M D: In the employment of conciliation (*sāman*), there is no loss, expenditure, or exertion; whereas in the case of force (*daṇḍa*), everything is indeed accomplished through its majesty. Therefore, these two are praised here. 7.110.
M D: An illustration of this is as follows: "Just as a wood-gatherer cuts down the brushwood yet protects the grain, so should the king protect his realm and slay those who stand in his way. (7.110)
The king who, out of delusion, oppresses his kingdom with total disregard shall, before long, fall from both his kingdom and his life, along with his kinsmen. (7.111)
Just as the vital breaths of living beings diminish through the emaciation of the body,
so too do the vital breaths of kings diminish through the emaciation of the kingdom.
M D: "For the kingdom is his body. Since this is so, therefore, in order to exclude those defects, he says [M: ...in order to set them aside... 7.110–12.
One should always observe this rule for the consolidation of the kingdom;
for a king whose kingdom is well-consolidated prospers in happiness. (7.113)
He should establish a *gulma* (military outpost) in the midst of two, three, or five [villages], and likewise for hundreds of villages, for the protection of the kingdom. (7.114)
For the purpose of collecting what belongs to the king and for the purpose of protection. 7.113–14.
One should appoint a lord of a village, as well as a lord of ten villages,
a lord of twenty, a lord of a hundred, and likewise a lord of a thousand.
The village headman himself should gradually report any faults that have arisen in the village to the leader of ten villages;
the leader of ten should report them to the leader of twenty.
The lord of twenty should report all of that to the lord of a hundred;
the lord of a hundred villages, in turn, should himself announce it to the lord of a thousand.
M D: The appointment of overseers in villages and other locations is set forth in three verses (7.115–17) for the purpose of making known the tasks that are at hand.
Whatever must be given daily to the king by the village dwellers—such as food, drink, fuel, and so forth—the village headman shall receive those. (7.118)
The officer of ten should enjoy one family; the officer of twenty, five families; the superintendent of a hundred villages, a village; and the lord of a thousand, a city.

M D: This conceptualization of the functions of the presiding deities has been stated in two verses [M: in two verses, their stations and activities are described according to their correspondence] (7.118–19).
Another minister of the king, one who is affectionate and vigilant, should oversee their village affairs as well as their private matters. (7.120)
The agent of the sovereign powers should observe, by way of action, that which has been done and left undone by them. (7.120)
In every city, he should appoint a single overseer of all affairs, stationed in a prominent place and formidable in appearance, like a planet among the stars. (7.121)
M D: In every city, he should appoint a municipal official endowed with a force consisting of elephants, horses, and other [troops]. || 7.121 ||
He himself should always personally inspect them all;
he should correctly ascertain their conduct throughout the realms by means of his spies. (7.122)
The king should always cause his governors to patrol for the sake of protection, and he should obtain information regarding their conduct from spies such as fraudulent ascetics. 7.122.

M D: For this reason: "For the king's officials appointed for protection generally become deceitful servants who seize the property of others; therefore, one should protect these subjects from them. (7.123)

M D: Even those who are pure consume wealth—meaning, because of the impermanence of the minds of men—therefore, they should not be disregarded on the grounds of an inference regarding their purity. || 7.123 ||
Those of evil intent who would seize wealth solely from those performing work for them—the king, having confiscated all their property, shall banish them. (7.124)

The king should cause those appointed officials who have committed known transgressions to be deprived of all their property and banished; the meaning is that this is for the purpose of protecting the realm. (7.124)
For women engaged in royal service and for the class of servants, he should provide a daily livelihood according to their rank and their work. (7.125)
The meaning is that it consists of such things as the preparation of clothing, anointing, and eating. || 7.125 ||
A paṇa should be given as wages for the low-born, and six for the high-born;
likewise, food and clothing every six months, and one droṇa of grain every month. (7.126)
M.D.: The preparation of the meal is described in two verses; he will state the measurements for the *paṇa* and the *droṇa*. 7.126.

Having carefully considered the buying and selling, the distance traveled, the food along with its incidental expenses, and the security of the goods, the king should cause taxes to be paid by the merchants. (7.127)
M: This is its general characteristic. D: This is its definition by way of generality. 7.127
Just as the king and the doer of deeds are joined with their fruit,
so should the king, having considered this, constantly determine the taxes within his realm.
Maitreya said: An illustration for this is as follows:
Just as calves, fish, and bees consume their food little by little, so too should the annual tax be collected from the kingdom by the king in small, small amounts. (7.129)
M D: This verse of illustration is for the purpose of praising the method of collecting taxes. || 7.129 ||
The king shall take a fiftieth part of cattle and gold;
an eighth part of grain, or a sixth, or even a twelfth. (7.130)
In the case of cattle and gold exceeding their value, a fiftieth part shall be taken. For grains, a specific portion [is to be determined] in consideration of the ease of collection. (7.130)
Furthermore, he may take a sixth part of trees, honey, clarified butter,
fragrant substances, medicinal herbs, juices, and of flowers, roots, and fruits.
And of leaf-vegetables, grasses, hides, and bamboo; of earthenware vessels and of everything made of stone. || 7.132 ||
M D: From the acquisition of the aforementioned trees and so forth, there is the taking of a sixth part [of the enjoyment]. 7.131–32.
Even when dying, a king shall not take a tax from a Śrotriya;
nor shall a Śrotriya dwelling within his realm perish from hunger.
M D: This is a deprecatory explanatory passage (arthavāda). 7.133.
In whose kingdom a man learned in the Vedas perishes from hunger, his realm likewise perishes from hunger before long. (7.134)
Having ascertained his learning and conduct, the king should provide him with a righteous livelihood;
he should protect him in every way, just as a father protects his own biological son. (7.135)
Whatever dharma he performs daily while being protected by the king, through that the king’s lifespan, wealth, and kingdom increase. (7.136)
M: Three verses concerning the welfare and requirements of one learned in the Vedas (*śrotriya*).
D: Three verses concerning the purpose of the superior welfare of two persons learned in the Vedas. (7.134–36)
Whatever little [tax] a common person living by trade in the kingdom might pay, the king shall cause it to be given as a tribute known as *kara* for the sake of the year. (7.137)

M D: A commoner other than a Brahmin, living by even a small amount of trade, must be made to pay taxes. (7.137) The king should cause artisans, craftsmen, and Śūdras who subsist by their own labor to perform work for one day every month. (7.138)
Those who subsist solely by their craft, as well as those who subsist for themselves, he shall compel to perform labor for one day each month. (7.138)
One should not cut off one's own root nor that of others through excessive greed;
for by cutting off one's own root, one afflicts both oneself and them. (7.139)
M: Thus, because of the prohibition regarding oneself, one should not cut off [the lineage] there for others.
D: Precisely because of that prohibition regarding both oneself and others, one should not cut off the *tantra*. 7.139.
A lord of the earth should be both harsh and mild, having considered the task at hand;
a king who is both harsh and mild becomes esteemed.
In brief, this conduct of kings should be constantly practiced. (7.140)
When weary from overseeing affairs, the king should appoint to that seat his chief minister—one who knows the Dharma, is wise, self-controlled, and of noble birth. (7.141)
MD: When weary from overseeing affairs, he should appoint the most excellent minister to the position of supervisor. 7.141.
Having thus performed all these duties incumbent upon himself, he should protect these subjects, remaining ever disciplined and vigilant. (7.142)
He from whose kingdom the subjects are being carried off—or oppressed—by bandits while he looks on, along with his ministers, is dead; he does not truly live. (7.143)
The supreme duty of a Kṣatriya is indeed the protection of his subjects; for a king who enjoys the fruits assigned to him is joined with righteousness through that very act. 7.144

And he who is disciplined, vigilant, and of unerring intellect should protect these subjects. These three verses concern the purpose and the explanatory praise (*arthavāda*) for the rule regarding the protection of the subjects. (7.142–44)
Having risen during the final watch of the night, having performed his purifications and being composed in mind,
and having offered oblations into the fires and honored the Brahmins, he should enter the auspicious assembly hall.
Remaining there, he should bid farewell to all his subjects with joy;
and having dismissed all his subjects, he should deliberate together with his ministers.
Together with his ministers, the king’s daily conduct is described in two verses (7.145–46).
Having ascended a mountain ridge or a palace, or having gone to a secluded place, or in a forest free from undergrowth, one should deliberate unobserved. (7.147)

M D: [M adds: "The ministers have been described; together with them"] he should deliberate on the five-limbed counsel (*mantra-pañcāṅga*). That is as follows: the means for the undertaking of actions, the excellence of personnel and materials, the division of place and time, the remedy for setbacks, and the accomplishment of the task. He should question them individually and collectively. Through reasoning, he should discern the distinctions in their opinions. Having achieved his objective, he should not let the right time pass, nor should he be one who deliberates too long. He should not deliberate on counsel with those who belong to the faction of those whom he might harm. And he should keep his counsel secret. (7.147)
By whose counsel ordinary people, having come together, do not know—
such a king enjoys the entire earth, even if he is destitute of treasure. (7.148)
And this being so, for the sake of protection:
"One should exclude from the mantra those who are dull-witted, blind, mute, or deaf; those born of animal wombs; those past their youth; women; barbarians; the diseased; and the deformed. (7.149)
M D:
Because those of animal birth, as well as women—especially the latter—betray a secret when treated with contempt; therefore, one should be careful in that regard. 7.150.
At midday or at midnight, being rested and free from fatigue, he should contemplate virtue, pleasure, and wealth, either alone or together with them. (7.151)
The king should contemplate the increase of dharma, artha, and kāma. When any one of these increases to the point of mutual conflict among kings, their destruction ensues. (7.150–51)
The acquisition of those things that are mutually contradictory, the giving away of daughters in marriage, and the protection of sons; || 7.152 ||

M D: When there is a mutual conflict among the ministers regarding *dharma*, *artha*, and *kāma*, one must consider their relative strength and weakness. The bestowal of maidens should be considered solely in light of the accomplishment of one's own purpose. The protection of princes must be ensured by means of secret agents (*sattrin*) who say, "We are yours," so that they may be made to accept *dharma* and *artha*. For a new substance, whatever kind of object it is smeared with, absorbs that very thing; in the same way, this prince of fresh intellect accepts whatever is said to him. By skillful means, they should turn him away from vices, and through constant instruction, the king should at the proper time establish him as the heir apparent (*yauvarājya*) when he is endowed with virtues, while relegating those lacking virtue to the border regions. Thus, by such exceptional application, the king should reflect daily upon the protection of his sons. (7.152)
The dispatching of messengers, as well as the remaining tasks to be done,
the movements within the inner apartments, and the activities of the spies.

M D: One should deliberate upon the dispatch of an envoy to that person with whom one intends to make peace or wage war. One should also consider the remaining tasks of an enterprise already begun, for the sake of its completion. Guarded by the troops of the inner harem (*antaḥvaṃśika*), he should enter the inner apartments (*antaḥpura*). There, he may see the Queen (*devī*) when she has been purified by elderly women, but not when she is unpurified. For a brother, lurking in the Queen’s chamber, killed Bhadrasena; a son, hidden within his mother’s bed, killed Kārūṣa; with an anklet smeared with poison, the Queen killed Vairantya; with the gem from her girdle, she killed Sauvīra; and with a weapon concealed in her braid, she killed Vidūratha. Therefore, he should carefully examine these vulnerable points. He should prohibit the association of the women of the inner apartments with shaven-headed ascetics, those with matted hair, sorcerers, and outside female slaves. And he should deliberate on the activities of spies, such as fraudulent agents (*kāpaṭika*), through a succession of secret reports. (7.153)
He [should know] in truth the entire eightfold work and the five groups,
as well as affection and enmity, and the conduct of the circle of states.

M.D.: Undertaking what has not been begun, the performance of what has been begun, the refinement of what has been performed, and the collection of the fruits of action; likewise, conciliation, sowing dissension, bribery, and force—this is the eightfold action (*karma*). Alternatively, agriculture, trade, waterworks, the construction of embankments, the improvement of what has already been built, the capture of elephants, digging and filling pits, the settling of uninhabited lands, and the clearing of forests—these are the activities. Others, however, say:
In taking up and in casting aside, likewise in commanding and in forbidding,
in the fifth case regarding the expression of purpose, and in the observation of legal proceedings.
Constantly engaged in the purification of punishment,
that king who possesses the eightfold course and performs the eight duties goes to heaven, honored by Śakra.

These are the two verses of Auśanas. Their commentary is as follows: 1. **Seizure** (*ādāna*): The taking of wealth from those who are powerful. 2. **Disbursement** (*visarga*): The distribution of wealth to servants. 3. **Command** (*praiṣa*): The dismissal of the wicked. 4. **Prohibition** (*niṣedha*): The restraint of excessive activity by those appointed over state affairs. 5. **Instruction** (*arthavacana*): The giving of counsel regarding improper conduct. 6. **Judicial Oversight** (*vyavahārekṣaṇa*): Supervision of legal proceedings so that those belonging to the various castes and stages of life (*varṇāśramiṇaḥ*) adhere to their own duties. 7. **Punishment** (*daṇḍanipātana*): The infliction of punishment upon those defeated in mutual litigation. 8. **Purification** (*śuddhi*): Purification of oneself; however, when there is a lapse due to negligence, there is **expiation** (*prāyaścitta*). These constitute the eightfold function of the king. The five-fold group (*pañcavarga*) consists of: the spy disguised as a fraudulent student (*kāpaṭika*), a renunciant (*udāsthita*), a householder (*gṛhapati*), a merchant (*vaidehaka*), and an ascetic (*tāpasa*). A *kāpaṭika* is a student (*chātra*) who knows the secrets of others and is bold. The minister, having won him over with wealth and honor, should say to him: "Taking the King and myself as your authority, whatever you see to be harmful in any matter, you must report it to us immediately, without letting anyone else hear it. An *udāsthita* is one who has fallen away from the life of a wandering mendicant (*pravrajyā*). He should be endowed with intelligence and purity. On land capable of providing all kinds of food, he should employ many disciples provided with abundant gold to perform labor. From the fruits of this agricultural work, he should provide for the food, clothing, and shelter of all wandering mendicants. Among them, those who desire a livelihood, he should instigate with these words: "In this very manner, the king’s interests must be served, and you must present yourselves at the time of receiving food and wages. All these wandering mendicants should, in turn, instigate their respective groups. A farmer whose means of subsistence have failed, but who is endowed with intelligence and purity, is a spy in the guise of a householder (*gṛhapati-vyañjana*). He should perform agricultural work on the aforementioned land. A merchant whose means of subsistence have failed, but who is endowed with intelligence and purity, is a spy in the guise of a merchant (*vaidehaka-vyañjana*). He should perform the work of trade on the designated land; the rest is the same as before. One who is bald or has matted hair, desiring a livelihood, is a spy in the guise of an ascetic (*tāpasa-vyañjana*). Near the city, with many disciples who are bald or wear matted hair, he should openly eat vegetables or a handful of grass every month or two months under the pretext of religious duty (*dharma*), while secretly consuming food as he pleases. His disciples, disguised as ascetics, should honor him with "perfected formulas" (*siddhayoga*). And his disciples should instruct him [of impending misfortune]: "There will be a fire today or tomorrow," "There will be danger from thieves," "There will be the execution or imprisonment of the wicked," or "This event will take place in a foreign land," or "The King will do this today or tomorrow. Then, his secret agents (*sattriṇaḥ*) dispatched by him should bring about these things. Furthermore, those who must necessarily be supported by the King should be secret agents (*sattriṇaḥ*) studying the science of marks (*lakṣaṇavidyā*), the science of limbs (*aṅgavidyā*), the science of sorcery (*jambhakavidyā*), the art of illusion (*māyāgata*), the duties of the stages of life (*āśramadharma*), and the knowledge of omens (*nimittajñāna*). In this regard, the King should station these five types of spies, along with these ministers, both in his own territory and in the territory of the enemy. He should dispatch secret agents among the minister, the domestic priest, the commander-in-chief, the crown prince, the doorkeeper, the chamberlain, and others—people who know trustworthy localities, dress, crafts, and languages—under the pretext of being commoners (*janapada*). Likewise, those disguised as hunchbacks, dwarfs, Kirātas, the mute, the dull-witted, the deaf, or the blind, as well as actors, dancers, singers, and women, should carry out internal surveillance.
In the forest, forest-dwellers such as ascetics and forest-hermits should be employed;
they must be swift and form a continuous chain of scouts for the purpose of knowing the activities of others.
These [spies] must be understood by the enemy as being of the same kind;
they consist of secret agents moving about on missions, both those known as "hidden" and those known as "open."

Having thus conceived of the fivefold group for both the enemy and oneself, one should likewise ascertain from this very [group] the loyalty or disloyalty of the ministers, domestic priests, and others; as well as the movements within the royal circle—namely, which regional ruler is engaged in what kind of conduct regarding peace, war, and so forth. (7.154)
One should diligently investigate the conduct of the middle king, the activities of the one seeking conquest, the movements of the neutral king, and those of the enemy as well. (7.155)

M.D.: In this circle of kings (*rājamaṇḍala*), these four constituent elements (*prakṛti*) are primary: the seeker of conquest (*vijigīṣu*), the enemy (*ari*), the middle king (*madhyama*), and the neutral king (*udāsīna*). Among them, that king who is endowed with the constituent elements and is emboldened by the thought, "I alone shall conquer this earth," is the seeker of conquest, owing to his possession of the power of energy (*utsāhaśakti*). The enemy is threefold: the natural (*sahaja*), the acquired (*prākṛta*), and the artificial (*kṛtrima*), as well as the one whose territory is immediately adjacent (*bhūmyanantara*). The middle king is one capable of subduing both the enemy and the seeker of conquest when they are not united. The neutral king is one capable of subduing the enemy, the seeker of conquest, and the middle king when they are not united, but not when they are united. (7.155)
In brief, these constituent elements are the root of the circle;
eight others are also enumerated, and thus they are traditionally known as twelve. (7.156)

These constituent elements (*prakṛti*) of the circle have been explained. Furthermore, for each of these constituent elements, two others are said to be its allies (*mitra*) and its ally’s ally (*mitramitra*). These eight, along with the one previously mentioned, are enumerated. Thus, there are twelve on both sides as well. (7.156)
The five others are known as the minister, the city, the realm, the treasury, and the army;
these are each described briefly, totaling seventy-two. (7.157)

M D: These five others—namely, the ministers (*amātya*), the city (*pura*), the realm (*rāṣṭra*), the treasury (*kośa*), and the army (*daṇḍa*)—are each established in twelve ways. Thus, there are twelve constituent elements of the king and sixty constituent elements beginning with the ministers; in brief, there are seventy-two. (7.157)
Immediately after [the conqueror], one should know the enemy and likewise the one who serves the enemy; next to the enemy is the ally, and beyond those two is the neutral party. (7.158)

M: One should know that the enemy of the seeker of victory (*vijigīṣu*) is the one whose territory is immediately adjacent; likewise, the friend of the enemy and the friend of the friend [are situated] beyond that. In this way, there are two others who become the friends of the seeker of victory. The neutral king (*udāsīna*) is further beyond those two. D: One should know that the enemy of the seeker of victory is the one whose territory is immediately adjacent. Likewise, [there are] the friend of the enemy and the friend of the friend of the enemy. In this way, the one whose territory is adjacent to the other side becomes the friend of the seeker of victory. The neutral king is further beyond those two. The definition of enemy and friend should be understood to apply to both natural (*sahaja*) and acquired (*kṛtrima*) relations. (7.158)
He should win over all of them by means of conciliation and other such expedients,
whether employed individually or collectively, through personal effort and statesmanship.

Whether by the four means beginning with conciliation, either collectively or individually, or by human policy alone, or by force alone—the phrase "by force alone" refers to the sequence of the six measures of royal policy (*ṣāḍguṇya*) as explained by Samāsika. (7.159)
He should always consider the six measures of policy: peace, war, marching, halting, dividing the army, and seeking refuge. (7.160)

M D: In this context, peace (*saṃdhi*) is that which is based on gold and other such things for the mutual benefit of both parties; its opposite is war (*vigraha*). Marching (*yāna*) is the superior advancement of one side. Remaining stationary (*āsana*) is indifference. Double-dealing (*dvaidhībhāva*) is the simultaneous adoption of both peace and war. Seeking refuge (*saṃśraya*) is surrendering oneself to another. One should always deliberate upon these six measures of policy (*ṣaḍguṇāḥ*). Among these six, whichever measure one considers capable of enabling one to build fortresses, capture elephants, dig mines, establish trade routes, settle uninhabited lands, promote agriculture, clear timber forests, or bring under cultivation fields not watered by rain—indeed, whatever such tasks one deems possible—and which would likewise thwart similar efforts of the enemy to obstruct one's growth, one should adopt that particular measure. (7.160)
This being so:
Having considered the task at hand, he should employ sitting in wait, marching forth, making peace, or waging war, as well as dividing his forces and seeking refuge. (7.161)

Having considered the task at hand, one should employ sitting after making peace (*saṃdhāyāsana*), sitting after declaring war (*vigṛhyāsana*), marching after making peace (*saṃdhāya yāna*), or marching after declaring war (*vigṛhya yāna*). Likewise, one may employ the double policy (*dvaidhībhāva*) or seeking protection (*saṃśraya*). When two enemies and conquerors (*arivijigīṣu*) desire to deceive each other but are unable to strike one another down, they may either sit after making peace or sit after declaring war. In that regard, when he perceives: "I am capable of weakening the enemy by my own strength; my constituent elements (*prakṛti*) are energetic, united, increased, and will carry out their duties without obstruction (and will strike at the enemy's tasks); or the enemy's constituent elements are greedy and depleted, such that they can be won over through instigation"—when he perceives such things, then he should sit after declaring war. In the absence of a reason for sitting after declaring war, he should sit after making peace. If he has gained superiority over the enemy, having made provisions within his own kingdom while excluding the entire mobilization of forces, he should march after declaring war; or when the enemy is in calamity, when his constituent elements are wasting away, or when they are provoked to rebellion; or when he possesses a rear-ally (*ākranda*) or a core force. However, in the absence of a reason for marching after declaring war, he should march after making peace with the rear-ally, or having entered into an agreement regarding the share of the fruit of the expedition with the rear-ally. Or, if he is capable, he may march after simultaneously declaring war against both the enemy and the rear-ally. Or, if he is incapable and attacked by a powerful foe, he should remain divided (*dvaidhībhūta*) by taking refuge in a fort; or he should seek shelter with the middle king (*madhyama*) or the neutral king (*udāsīna*); or he should resort to whichever course was practiced by his ancestors, or to where there are close relatives or many friends who are capable of providing aid. (7.161)
A king should know that there are two kinds of alliance as well as conflict; likewise, both marching and encamping, as well as the double policy and seeking refuge. (7.162)
Maitreya: These six qualities, in brief, are divided into two types; for this presentation is made for the purpose of what is to be explained hereafter. (7.162)
When the undertaking of the journey is common and likewise the opposite, then that treaty, connected with future consequences, should be known as having two characteristics. (7.163)

A treaty in which the means of transport (*yāna*) is common to both parties is one where the action regarding the transport is shared; this is a "treaty with common transport. A treaty in which the action regarding the transport is not shared—such as "you go from here" and "I shall go from there"—is its opposite, a "treaty with non-common transport. Likewise, through the acquisition of treasury and other resources, one party is provided for in the present while the other is provided for in the future. In this way, this treaty comes to possess two characteristics. (7.163)
War is said to be of two kinds: that waged by oneself for the sake of one's own body, either at an improper time or at the proper time, and that waged because a friend has been wronged. (7.164)

M D: When one is capable of defeating an enemy by one's own power, then it is a war undertaken by oneself; even at an improper time, it is undertaken out of a desire for accumulation [i.e., for one's own advancement]. When an enemy of another is a friend of the one seeking victory (*vijigīṣu*), and that enemy of the other inflicts harm upon him, then—when the enemy of the seeker of victory has been harmed by that friend, or when the enemy is in distress—it is a "contrary" war (*viparīta-vigraha*). When the causes for war exist, whether there is staying put (*āsana*) or marching (*yāna*), war is always of two kinds. (7.164)
When an urgent matter has arisen by chance, marching alone or in alliance with a friend—these two types of marching are prescribed. (7.165)

Marching alone against an enemy when he is in distress or when an urgent matter has arisen, provided that he is capable of defeating him while alone; or marching together with an ally when one is incapable—thus is twofold marching. 7.165.
When one's power has gradually diminished due to fate or past actions, or out of consideration for a friend, neutrality (āsana) is declared to be of two kinds. 7.166.

And even one who acts rightly goes to ruin through fate, while another does so through the aforementioned negligence; for one who has thus perished in either way, the posture of remaining stationary (*āsana*) is for the sake of self-restraint. Furthermore, he who is an enemy to another is a friend to one desiring victory; when that [enemy] is ruined, one should remain seated even if capable, out of consideration for him. Thus, there are two kinds of *āsana*. There is another reading of the reason: "through delusion or by what was done previously. (7.166)

The maintenance of both the army and the master for the sake of accomplishing the task is declared to be of two kinds as "dual policy" by those who know the qualities of the six measures of statecraft. (7.167)

One who has been overwhelmed by a powerful enemy and has taken refuge in a fortress should accomplish his own purpose by employing a two-fold strategy regarding his forces. Or, if he is capable of favoring others, he should assist another king with a certain portion of his army, in expectation of results such as firewood and other resources. || 7.167 ||

Seeking refuge for the sake of accomplishing one's purpose while being oppressed by enemies, and not being falsely accused among the virtuous—these two are recorded as the types of seeking refuge. (7.168)

When one is oppressed by a great enemy, one should seek refuge with a powerful protector; and having sought refuge, one should serve him with every effort to accomplish his own purpose—even if one is a sinner—so as not to bring reproach upon the virtuous. One may seek refuge due to a calamity that necessitates such dependence. For one who has thus sought refuge becomes invincible to his peers at that time.
When one perceives that there will certainly be a great advantage for oneself in the future, and only a slight hardship in the present, then one should resort to peace. (7.169)
D: [M omits] Looking toward the future, one should resort to peace after inflicting only slight injury upon oneself. 7.169.
When he perceives that all his subjects are exceedingly joyful, then he should consider himself to have achieved success in war. (7.170)

M: One who desires victory, honored by the excellence of all his constituent elements, well-satisfied, and having secured his subjects, should wage war. D: One who is exalted by the excellence of the army and other resources for the purpose of war, being satisfied and having secured his subjects, should engage in both peace and war. (7.170)
When he perceives his own force to be joyful and robust in spirit, and that of the enemy to be the opposite, then he should march against the foe. (7.171)
M: When one's own forces are flourishing and strong while those of the enemy are the opposite for some reason, one should march forth after either declaring war or making peace.

D: When others are in a state contrary to one's own—being both joyful and well-provisioned due to their own exclusive causes—one should march forth, either after declaring war or after making peace. 7.171.
But when he is completely depleted of both mounts and troops,
then he should sit with diligence, gradually conciliating the enemy.

When his gold and other resources are exhausted, he should remain focused on achieving his own advancement by conciliating the enemy through the means of conciliation (*sāman*) and the bestowal of gifts (*upapradāna*). || 7.172 ||
When the king considers his enemy to be stronger in every respect, then,
having divided his army into two parts, he should accomplish his own purpose.
When overcome by a powerful foe and unable to hold his ground, he should take refuge in a fortress and remain there, having divided his forces into two parts. || 7.173 ||
But when he becomes most vulnerable to the forces of the enemy, then he should quickly seek refuge with a righteous and powerful king. (7.174)

M D: Even if one resorts to a state of double-dealing, if one considers self-preservation impossible, then before being overcome, one should quickly seek refuge with a powerful and righteous king; in his absence, with another who possesses good qualities. (7.174)
One should always serve with every effort that person who effects the suppression of both the subjects and the enemy's forces, just as one would serve a teacher. 7.175

When a person has become most difficult to approach due to the fault of certain dispositions, one should serve him with all efforts, relying upon the highest sincerity with an unobstructed mind, provided that one is capable of restraining those dispositions and his enemies. || 7.175 ||
If he should perceive even there a fault arising from taking refuge, then, free from hesitation, he should engage in fair combat itself. (7.176)

For kings, seeking refuge with a relative or a powerful ally is indeed a great fault; thus, if he should bring about ruin through such a course of seeking refuge, then he should engage in fair combat even in that situation, free from hesitation. Indeed, it is observed that even one of small strength may conquer one of great strength. Furthermore, even defeat for one who fights is distinguished by the attainment of heaven; however, one who relies on a visible refuge finds no favor either in this world or the next. (7.176)
M D: In short, a king who understands policy should employ every means such that his friends, neutrals, and enemies do not become superior to him. (7.177)

M.D.: Through the lure of wealth and other such things, even a friend turns into an enemy; what then need be said of a neutral person or an enemy? Therefore, by employing the aforementioned means and setting them in motion, one should make oneself appear more attractive to friends and others than they are to themselves, and one should not place reliance on whether someone is a friend or neutral. (7.177)

One should examine the future of all undertakings as well as their present state, and the merits and defects of all past ones in accordance with reality. (7.178) Because undertakings have many facets and are momentary, a particular task arises in each respective stage; thus, he demonstrates the general determination of all tasks. (Why is this so? Because it is said: "In the first place, the merits and defects regarding all tasks must be understood in relation to the future. (7.178) [See commentary on 7.179 in D.]
M: This being so, D: therefore it is again thus, because:
"One who knows the virtues and faults regarding the future, and who possesses immediate certainty regarding the present," [M: determination].
One who knows the remnants of past actions is not overcome by enemies. || 7.179 ||

M: When one begins an action that is free from defects, then its result will be excellent by virtue of its own inherent qualities. At that time, the merits and defects are to be understood. One who is free from defects is quickly determined to be capable of the task; therefore, he should be employed. Regarding a past action, there is reliance on the remainder of the work...
D: For the future, the merits and defects in all actions must be understood; as for the determination of the remainder...

And its application is for the sake of favoring the royal administration by avoiding faults; thus, it results in the destruction of one's enemies. Like armor, it should be constantly contemplated by the seeker of victory as accompanying all undertakings. (7.179)
He should arrange everything in such a way that his allies, neutrals, and enemies do not deceive him; this is the summary of political strategy.
M D: This verse is for the purpose of a summary. 7.180.
But when the lord intends to set out toward the enemy's kingdom, he should then proceed slowly toward the enemy's city according to this following rule. (7.181)
Maitreya said: "The presentation of the journey is for the purpose of directing the mind. (7.181)
In the auspicious month of Mārgaśīrṣa, the lord of the earth should set out on his expedition,
or else toward the months of Phālguna or Caitra, according to his strength.

For in this case, while marching, one destroys another's autumn and spring crops; furthermore, the roads for those marching become abundant in fodder and water. Therefore, one should march against a territory where the autumn harvest predominates during the month of Mārgaśīrṣa for a long-term expedition; and against a territory where the spring harvest predominates during the months of Phālguna and Caitra for a long-term expedition. Likewise, one with a fourfold army should march in Mārgaśīrṣa, but one whose strength primarily consists of cavalry should march in Phālguna and Caitra. (7.182)
Moreover, at other times as well, when he perceives certain victory, he should march forth after declaring war, or when a calamity has arisen for the enemy. (7.183)

A king whose army consists primarily of elephants should march against an enemy whose army consists primarily of horses during the rainy season; for when one marches during this time of one's own strength, victory for the king is certain. Furthermore, he may march at some time when the enemy is in distress, provided he is capable of doing so and the enemy has no allies to call upon. (7.183)

Having performed the ritual arrangements at the base according to the rules, as well as those pertaining to the journey, and having secured a place of residence and properly established a system of scouts; (7.184)

MD: The maintenance of the constituent elements (*prakṛti*) by means of wealth and honor; the protection of those who are greedy or angry, especially the securing of the rear-enemy (*pārṣṇigrāha*); the establishment of the countryside and the fortification of the base (the protection of the root, consisting of such things as the preparation of the capital city and the like); and the expeditionary force (*yātrika*), such as elephants and horses. Furthermore, those who are disaffected (*dūṣya*) in the enemy's territory become the expedition leader’s foothold (*āspada*). Having won them over and having properly established spies for the purpose of gaining accurate knowledge of activities in the enemy's territory—just as this is so—[7.184].
Having cleared the three types of paths and assessed his own sixfold strength,
he should advance slowly toward the enemy's city according to the rules for a campaign.

Having cleared the three types of terrain—the arid, the marshy, and the intermediate—by securing fodder, fuel, water, and by cutting through thickets and other obstacles; and having cleared the sixfold army consisting of elephants, horses, chariots, infantry, porters, and the treasury; and having determined what has been carried forward and what remains behind according to the rules for future contingencies and the rules for immediate needs, he should march with the intent to fight. (7.185)
One should be especially vigilant toward a friend who serves one's enemies and remains hidden, as well as toward one who goes and returns; for such a person is indeed the most dangerous enemy.
Having become more closely associated with one who has gone away in sorrow due to a friend and has now returned, one should especially not place trust in him. 7.186.
He should march along that path in the staff formation, or the wagon formation, or the boar, the eagle, the needle, or the crocodile formation. (7.187)

The commander-in-chief is in the front, the general and the sovereign are behind; in the center are the elephants, and on both flanks are the horses—this is the arrangement of vehicles for battle. When there is danger from all sides, the *daṇḍavyūha* (staff-array) should be formed as a long, even deployment. When there is danger from the rear, the *śakaṭavyūha* (cart-array), which is narrow at the front and wide at the back, should be employed. The *varāhavyūha* (boar-array), which has a smooth front and rear half and a broad middle, is recommended when there is danger from the flanks. By this, the *garuḍavyūha* (eagle-array) is explained. The *sūcīvyūha* (needle-array) consists of troops capable of rapid mobilization, long and with brave men at its head; it is most effective when there is danger in front. The *makaravyūha* (crocodile-array), which is broad at the head and tail, is recommended when there is danger from both sides. || 7.187 ||
And from whichever side the danger arises, from that side he should extend his force;
he himself, however, should always take up his position in the lotus array.
M D: This is a general instruction: wherever one perceives danger, there one should extend the force; one should always encamp in a lotus-array (padmavyūha) facing in all directions. || 7.188 ||
The commander-in-chief and the army supervisor should station themselves in all directions;
and from whichever direction he suspects danger, he should designate that as the eastern quarter.

The generals, commanders, and men should take up positions everywhere. Other various types of stratagems have been devised to defeat the enemy; therefore, it is appropriate that men be employed for this purpose. Having placed a mountain or a forest behind them and facing the direction from which danger arises in front, they should either fight or take up their positions there. (7.189)
And he should station trusted troops as outposts on all sides—men skilled in both their positions and in battle, who are fearless and unswerving. (7.190)

M D: In cases of abdominal tumors (gulma), those possessing such qualities should especially be appointed; for from them arises fear that leads to great misfortune through one's own power. || 7.190 ||
One should cause a few warriors to fight in a compact formation, but one may extend many as desired;
having arrayed them in the needle or the thunderbolt formation, one should cause them to fight.

A small number of men, when closely arrayed and fighting with mutual regard for one another, do not fear. The *vajra* (thunderbolt) array is established in three parts. The *sūcī* (needle) array has already been explained. However, all arrays should be arranged according to one's capability. 7.191.
One should fight with chariots and horses on level ground; likewise, on marshy ground, with boats and elephants;
and in places covered by trees and shrubs, with forces armed with bows, swords, shields, and other weapons.
M D: This instruction is for the purpose of demonstrating capability. 7.192.
He should cause the Kaurukṣetras, the Matsyas, the Pāñcālas, and those born in Śūrasena—men who are both tall and short—to fight in the vanguard ranks. (7.193)
For these broad-chested men, with arms reaching to their knees, touching the heavens, and of great stature, cause a slight mental affliction to their enemies at the heads of the armies. (7.193)
He should cheer his army, properly inspect the battle array, and also discern the movements of the enemies as they fight. (7.194)

One should gladden them by demonstrating the meaning of the treatise as it truly is, according to such passages as: "In victory there is dharma and wealth; in defeat there is liberation" [or "in defeat there is heaven"]. One should also observe the actions of those engaged in battle; for men whose minds are fickle may cause harm even to one who is helping them. (7.194)
Having besieged the enemy, he should remain there and harass his kingdom;
he should constantly corrupt his supplies of fodder, food, water, and fuel. (7.195)
He should break down tanks as well as walls and moats; he should launch a surprise attack upon him at night and terrify him. (7.196)
He should instigate those who can be instigated and remain ever aware of their actions;
intent on fate, he should fight with his fear departed, desiring victory. (7.197)
M D: The method of besieging one who has taken refuge in a stronghold and is not fighting back is explained in three verses (7.195–97).
One should strive to conquer enemies through conciliation, bribery, sowing dissension, or by all these means combined or individually; one should never fight them in battle. (7.198)

In that regard, conciliation (*sāman*) is twofold: the application of speech and the application of gesture. The application of speech consists of speaking of virtues, speaking of what is beneficial, speaking of the observation of benefits, self-surrender, and so forth. The application of gesture consists of joining the palms while standing, taking the hand, showing a smiling face, showing one's own wife, conversing together, and so forth. Generosity (*dāna*) is the production of affection through various kinds of material objects. Sowing dissension (*bheda*) is the winning over of one person and the alienation of another, as well as intimidation. One should strive to conquer by means of these three methods. (7.198)
Since victory is seen to be uncertain for two who fight, and defeat likewise occurs in battle, one should therefore avoid war. (7.199)
M D: Since victory and defeat are uncertain, one should avoid battle through diligent effort. Therefore, even a small matter that is certain is better than a great matter that is doubtful. 7.199.
If even the three previously mentioned expedients are not possible, he should fight with such diligence and exertion that he may conquer his enemies. (7.200)

M D: When the means such as conciliation (*sāman*) have failed for one who desires victory, war is the effective means. Likewise, when victory is uncertain, one may indeed fight, because there is material gain in victory and heaven in defeat; thus, in that case, war itself is superior. But when defeat is certain regarding material gain, then fleeing is better; for one who has fled can again achieve his purpose. 7.200.
Having conquered, he should worship the gods and righteous Brahmins;
he should grant exemptions and proclaim amnesties of safety. (7.201)
But having understood the intended purpose of all these people in brief, he should install a member of their own lineage there and establish a covenant. (7.202)
And he should establish authoritative standards for them and their appropriate duties;
he should honor these men with jewels, together with the principal officials. (7.203)
Maitreya said: These three verses are for the purpose of pacifying that which has been attained. (7.201–03)
Non-giving is disagreeable, while giving brings about what is agreeable;
the timely bestowal of desired objects is highly praised. (7.204)

Giving or even non-giving, when joined with the proper time, brings happiness; therefore, when performed by a king at the appropriate time, it becomes a source of happiness for the entire world. (7.204)
All this action is dependent upon the two ordinances, the divine and the human;
of these two, the divine is indeed inconceivable, whereas in the human there exists effort.

M: As for that which is human fruit, it depends solely on human action (*puruṣakarman*), such as agriculture and the like. Furthermore, even that fruit which is obtained through fate (*daiva*), such as the birth of a son and so forth, likewise functions only through a visible medium. Therefore, one should strive toward every undertaking by relying exclusively on visible means; one should not remain inactive, making fate the supreme authority. 7.205.
Or, being disciplined, he may even march together with him after having carefully made a treaty, perceiving the threefold fruit consisting of allies, gold, or land. (7.206)

But this act of making friends is the fruit of the expedition against the enemy; having conquered him, one should establish him [in his own position]. Thinking, "Having acted as an ally, he will protect [the territory] and, having become a friend, will perform the duties of a friend at the proper time," one should either conclude a treaty with him for land and gold and then withdraw, or [act otherwise]. (7.206)
Having carefully observed the rear-attacker and the ally within the circle of states, one may obtain the fruit of an expedition from either a friend or even an enemy. (7.207)

Having considered the consequences of the cries of those who have become rear-enemies, one should collect gold and other wealth where it is not productive; for by collecting it without due consideration, one becomes the perpetrator of the fault resulting from that act. (7.207)

A king does not prosper so much upon acquiring land filled with gold as he does by gaining a firm friend, even if that friend is currently weak, provided he is capable of enduring for the future. (7.208)
A light friend who knows the dharma, is grateful, has a joyful disposition, is devoted, and is steadfast in his undertakings is highly praised. (7.209)
M D: With two verses beginning "Better than land and gold is a friend," there is praise of that [friend], for the purpose of winning over a friend. 7.208–09.
The wise say it is a painful thing to have as an enemy one who is intelligent, of noble birth, brave, skillful, generous, grateful, and steadfast. (7.210)

M D: The purpose of this instruction is as follows: one who desires victory should form an alliance with such an enemy by all possible means, so that even one possessing such qualities can be destroyed, weakened, or oppressed. Therefore, one should diligently seek to make such an enemy a friend. (7.210)
Nobility, knowledge of men, heroism, and a compassionate nature; constant magnanimity and the arising of the qualities of one who remains impartial—these are his traits. (7.211)

M.D.: The word *udaya* denotes a collective (*samudāya*). However, its meaning as "result" (*phala*) is not appropriate here, due to the force of the context. The purpose of this instruction is as follows: having relied upon a neutral king (*udāsīna*) endowed with these qualities, one may even oppose an enemy possessing the characteristics previously described for the sake of achieving the results of a military expedition (*yātrā*). It is by virtue of such qualities that a neutral king becomes capable of performing the duties of a protector. A neutral king lacking these qualities, however, becomes an adversary through the instigation of enemies, owing to his lack of firm wisdom. [7.211] M: *anenaivaṃguṇenaivaṃguṇas* (the manuscript reads *anenaivaṃguṇenaivaṃguṇas*, though the commentary suggests *anenaivaṃguṇenaivaṃguṇas*); however, the reading *prajñatayā* (omitting *tasya*) is preferred. || 7.211 ||
A king should unhesitatingly abandon even a land that is secure, always productive of crops, and conducive to the increase of cattle, for the sake of his own self-interest. (7.212)

But when a king desiring victory finds himself in such a situation due to an attack by an enemy, he should then seek refuge with a neutral power; at that time, the king should abandon even a land that is secure, productive of crops, and constantly conducive to the increase of cattle—even though it possesses such qualities—since it is thus prescribed in the duties of kings: 7.212. [The king should abandon] even such a land as this, for it is so remembered in the royal codes of conduct.
Wealth should be preserved for times of misfortune; a wife should be protected even with wealth;
but one's own self must always be protected, even at the cost of both wife and wealth. (7.213)

M.D.: "One must always protect oneself even by the renunciation of everything. For it was by this [means] that he, though capable [of other ways], abandoned his wife—even though it was contrary to *dharma*—and having regained his kingship once more, was able to perform great religious duties (*dharmānuṣṭhāna*). However, for no king other than him is it proper to protect himself by abandoning his wife; for what other virtuous deed (*satkarma*) could he have performed after abandoning his wife that would have preserved his soul or avoided public reproach? And so it has been said: "And [an act] that is censured by the world... (4.176). This was done by him through acts such as worship, because he possessed realized knowledge and had lost his wealth—not merely by following the instruction on royal duties. (7.213)
Having thoroughly observed all calamities that have arisen together, the wise man should employ every means, both those that are joined and those that are separate. (7.214)

Having closely observed all calamities—both divine and human—that have arisen together in great force, the wise man should employ all possible means, beginning with conciliation, either collectively for all three or two at a time, or individually when they are separated; he should neither act precipitously nor fall into despondency. This is the meaning. (7.214)
M: He summarizes that [teaching] in brief by means of his own intuition, without depending on instructions. D:
He summarizes that [teaching] by way of setting forth his own primordial natures (*prakṛti*):
the attainer, the goal to be attained, and all the means in their entirety.
Relying upon these three, one should strive for the accomplishment of one's purpose.
MD: Because states are infinite, this presentation of all means in brief should be understood as being for the purpose of self-protection [or: for the sake of establishing the self]. || 7.215 ||
Having thus deliberated on all this with his ministers, the king, after exercising and bathing at midday, should proceed to the inner apartments to eat. (7.216)
M D: This verse is for the purpose of summary. 7.216.

There, he should eat food that has been thoroughly examined by attendants who are like his own self, who know the proper time, who cannot be led astray, and who use mantras that dispel poison. (7.217)
He should combine all his belongings with water that destroys poison, and, being self-controlled, he should always wear jewels that counteract poison. (7.218)
And women who have been tested by means of ointments, water, and incense, being well-composed and adorned with their dress and ornaments, should touch him. (7.219)
In this manner, one should exert effort regarding vehicles, beds, food, and seats;
likewise in bathing, grooming, and all matters concerning ornaments. (7.220)
Having eaten, he should likewise enjoy himself with the women in the inner apartments; and having enjoyed himself at the proper time, he should again consider his duties. (7.221)
And having adorned himself, he should inspect the armed men once more, as well as all the mounts, weapons, and ornaments. (7.222)
Having performed the twilight devotions, he should remain armed within his inner apartments and listen to the reports of those who disclose secrets and to the activities of his spies.
Having gone to another inner chamber and dismissed those people, he should enter the inner apartments again, surrounded by women, for the purpose of eating. (7.224)
Having eaten there a little more, gladdened by the sounds of musical instruments, he should go to bed at the proper time and rise with his fatigue dispelled. (7.225)
A healthy lord of the earth should carry out this entire conduct;
but when unwell, he should entrust all of this to his servants. 7.226

M.D.: From the verse beginning with "having exercised and bathed" (*vyāyamyāplutya*) onwards, these eleven verses concerning the protection of the self during recreation (*vaihārika-ātmasaṃrakṣaṇa*) are well known and are therefore not commented upon. Thus, having established the system of government and secured his own safety, the king should oversee legal proceedings for the accomplishment of the affairs of his subjects. (7.217–26)
Thus ends the seventh chapter in the *Manuśāstravivaraṇa*, the work of Ṛjuvimala.

M: Thus ends the seventh chapter of the *Smṛtimīmāṃsā*, a commentary on the *Manuśāstra*, composed by Bhāruci, the author of the *Ṛjuvimalā*, who was a disciple of the venerable Ācārya Nartakīya, whose memory is praiseworthy and who has attained union with [the divine].
Chapter Eight. M D:

Thus, having properly established the machinery of government according to the principles of royal science taught in the seventh chapter, the king, desiring to oversee legal proceedings for the sake of protecting his subjects, [should sit] together with Brāhmaṇas.
Instructed by ministers who are experts in counsel, he should enter the assembly hall.

Māndhātṛ said: For the sake of maintaining the stability of the world by preventing the "law of the fish" (*mātsyanyāya*), this king—who is habitually disposed toward investigating legal proceedings—should sit together with Brāhmaṇas, those whom he will describe later in the verse beginning, "In whatever place three Brāhmaṇas learned in the Vedas sit," and with them [the ministers]. For it is they who are given this qualification: "those who know the *mantras*. Thus, even if they are learned in the Vedas, if they do not also know the *mantras*, this qualification is provided for the purpose of attaining an additional characteristic. Those who know the worldly conduct of affairs are the "knowers of *mantras*. And the phrase "with ministers who are knowers of *mantras*" shares the same preceding qualification. However, there is this distinction: ministers are required by necessity to be experts in the administrative conduct of the royal government, whereas in the other case (the Brāhmaṇas), there is no such prohibition. Therefore, he qualifies them in this way as well. "Disciplined, he should enter the court. Disciplined means one whose dress and ornaments are not ostentatious. The "court" is that which will be described later: "They know that to be the court of Brahmā. And although a Brāhmaṇa possesses the status of a teacher of dharma and a spiritual preceptor (*guru*), he is not made the primary authority in the administration of justice. For he is incapable of subduing wrongdoers because of his small circle of dependents and lack of resources. But for a Kṣatriya, since his duty is the protection of the subjects through the collection of taxes, tributes, favors, enjoyments, and fines, his possession of great resources is understood from his livelihood and purpose; thus, he has the capacity to restrain wrongdoers for the sake of protecting the subjects. This being so, the Kṣatriya is designated as the primary authority in the administration of justice. Alternatively, the instruction for the Kṣatriya to administer justice may have an invisible (transcendental) purpose. "Legal proceeding" (*vyavahāra*) is the act of transacting (*vyavaharaṇa*). Here, one person transacts for his own sake, while another transacts otherwise; thus, there is a manifold variety of transactions. Or, "legal proceeding" is the mutual contesting of opposing claims against one another. (8.1)
Seated there or even standing, having raised his right hand and being modest in dress and ornaments, he should examine the legal cases of the litigants.

M.D.: Sitting, he should look upon other people—excluding ascetics, learned Brahmins, and gurus; or even standing, he should look upon those of the highest castes, beginning with ascetics. The mention of the hand is intended to indicate the arm. For this is a court of Brahman (a court of the aged). And so it has been said regarding the fire-sanctuary and other such places: [the raising of the right arm]. Indeed, petitioners will approach the king with ease when his dress and ornaments are modest. Alternatively, this is a rule for him that serves an unseen purpose (*adṛṣṭa-prayojana*), for the sake of the meaningfulness of the scripture. Since he should look in this manner at the legal cases of petitioners, and not produce cases himself—cases in which the efficacy of scriptural instruction is not observed—it is understood that this instruction regarding the examination of legal disputes concerns only petitioners. This being the case, its status as a non-injunction (*avidhitva*) is established. Otherwise, there would be no restrictive exclusion (*parisaṃkhyā*) of instruction regarding others who are like his own dependents. Furthermore, when an injunction is possible, a restrictive exclusion is not appropriate. Nor can a single instruction have efficacy in both respects, because a sentence has but a single meaning. Thus, the examination of legal disputes by Brahmins and others in their own households remains unprohibited. Now, he will say later, "He should not himself produce a case," and "Neither should his servant. Therefore, this [present statement] is merely a restatement (*anuvāda*) of that, to be understood here as a contextual elaboration (*prasaṅga*). Or rather, let this be an original instruction (*upadeśa*) here for its own sake, while the subsequent [statement] is a restatement for the sake of specification: "Nor should his servant [produce a case]. (8.2)

Regarding what was stated, "He shall oversee the affairs of those who have business," the reason for this must be explained; therefore, this [section] is commenced for the purpose of establishing that reason:
"Day by day, by means of reasons observed in local custom and observed in the scriptures, [the king] shall examine separately each of the eighteen titles of law. (8.3)

M.D.: Regarding the eighteen paths of legal procedure (*vyavahāra-sthāna*), such as the non-payment of debts and others to be described hereafter—which are established separately for each—the king, without growing weary day by day, shall examine the cases of litigants according to the customs of the country (*deśācāra-vyavasthā*) among farmers, merchants, herdsmen, and others, and according to the rules of the treatises (*śāstra-vyavasthā*) by means of the reasons stated in the scriptures, such as witnesses and oaths. Although there are worldly signs (*liṅga*) mentioned in the scriptures, such as: “One should discern [the truth] by external signs” (*bāhyair vibhāvayel liṅgaiḥ*) and “In this way, by inference, the king should reach the state of dharma” (*tathānumānena nayed dharmasya nṛpatiḥ padam*), nevertheless, this [verse] is a restatement (*anuvāda*) of worldly means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*). However, the scriptural definition of proof consists of witnesses, oaths, and so forth. And although there is a restatement of worldly means of knowledge in this treatise for some reason, nevertheless, in certain matters, the scripture makes the world itself the authority (*pramāṇa*). Thus he will say: “Those skilled in sea-voyages, those who see the meaning of regions and local dialects,” and so forth. Therefore, the separate mention of “country” (*deśa*) is appropriate. (8.3)
And these bases of legal procedure (vyavahāravastu) are now set forth:

among them, the first is the non-payment of debt (ṛṇādāna), followed by deposits (nikṣepa), sale without ownership (asvāmivikraya), partnerships (saṃbhūyasamutthāna), and the non-delivery of what has been given (dattānapakarma). (8.4)
Non-payment of wages, breach of contract, rescission of purchase and sale, and disputes between owners and herdsmen; 8.5.
The law concerning boundary disputes, verbal and physical assault, theft, violence, and the abduction of women; 8.6.
The duties of husband and wife, partition [of inheritance], gambling, and betting—these eighteen are the titles of law established here in this world. (8.7)

M.D.: Here, the subject matter of the dispute is presented in four verses. The first is the primary one. For this legal proceeding concerning debt touches even forest-dwellers; therefore, its primacy is stated. (8.4–7)
In these matters, he should resolve the legal cases of men who are mostly engaged in disputes by relying upon the eternal Dharma. 8.8.

MD: These are the primary subjects of legal procedure (*vyavahāra-vastu*). Because their subdivisions are infinite, it is impossible to provide a complete enumeration of them. Furthermore, by the use of the term "most frequently," the great number of these subjects of legal procedure is understood. Even regarding matters not explicitly mentioned, one should determine the case by relying on eternal law (*dharma*) through wisdom that follows the scriptures. One should set aside even those practices established by fathers and grandfathers if they are unjust, for people generally follow what has been done before, especially kings. Therefore, this effort is undertaken; this instruction is general, while its specific details will be stated in their proper context. (8.8)
But when the king himself does not personally oversee the legal proceedings, then he should appoint a learned Brāhmaṇa to oversee those proceedings. (8.9)

But when, due to some other circumstance, the king himself does not perceive the matter, then he should appoint a learned Brāhmaṇa to oversee the case, and not one of another caste—even if the latter is knowledgeable in dharma and conversant with legal procedure—provided that even the Brāhmaṇa is learned specifically in those scriptures to be known by Brāhmaṇas. It is stated [in this regard] for the purpose of ensuring that he does not transgress the duties incumbent upon him: "His learning is declared [to be restricted] to those scriptures to be known by Brāhmaṇas, so as not to overstep their duties. However, his learning regarding the judicial process is not subject to such restriction, because it is acquired through the practical requirements of the matter itself. (8.9)
M: He, surrounded by exactly three members of the court, should oversee his duties;
or, when the king is unwell in body or preoccupied with other affairs, he should enter the foremost assembly hall himself.
M: [He should do so] elsewhere than that; and not having ascended the royal throne in the assembly hall. What then? Seated or even standing in the very assembly hall of the court. 8.10.

M: Thus, the purpose for the alternation between standing and sitting has been stated. Those who are virtuous in the assembly are the *sabhya*s; and they, possessing the aforementioned qualifications, should indeed belong to an assembly of Brahmins situated in a formal gathering (*samāja*).
D: "Surrounded by three *sabhya*s, he should oversee his duties, having entered the foremost assembly hall, either seated or standing. (8.10)

D: When the king is unwell in body or preoccupied with other affairs, he should enter the assembly hall itself and [sit] at the head, and not elsewhere; nor even in the assembly hall should he ascend the royal throne, but rather remain in the assembly hall seated on another seat. Regarding "seated or standing," there is an option between standing and sitting. The purpose has been stated. Those who are virtuous in the assembly are the *sabhyas* (members of the court); and they, possessing the aforementioned qualifications, should indeed be assistants to the Brahmin acting in the capacity of the king. 8.10.
It has been stated that "the assembly is the foremost"; for this reason, the following is said:
"In whatever place three Brahmins learned in the Vedas sit together, along with a learned minister of the king, they know that assembly to be a Brahma-sabhā. (8.11)

M: Because of the mention of the *tri* (the three), they would not be those who do not know the Veda; and by the logic of the "stick and cake" (*daṇḍāpūpika*), even four—or indeed many—are not contradictory. Furthermore, the statement that he is "learned and a natural assistant to the king" is a restatement (*anuvāda*) for the sake of what follows. Some read "brāhmaṇa" instead of "brahmaṇas," saying "they know that assembly of the Brāhmaṇa"; but that is incorrect, because this has already been stated regarding his caste: "Then one should appoint a learned Brāhmaṇa to oversee the legal proceedings" (in the previous section). The mention of "brahmaṇas" is appropriate for the purpose of praising the assembly, as in the expression "the assembly of Brahmā" (just as there is a "secular assembly"). Alternatively, since it was said that "one should enter the assembly modestly," this is stated as a defining characteristic (*upalakṣaṇa*) of that place where they sit, and so forth, in order to exclude secular assemblies. 8.11.
When Dharma, pierced by Adharma, stands before an assembly, and the members of that assembly do not extract the dart, they themselves are pierced. (8.12)

"Dharma" refers to the administration of justice according to the scriptures. Its "piercing" (*vedha*) is the judging otherwise. The fruit of this—namely, the cause for the collapse of the established order of *dharma*—is stated here with reference to the appointed Brahmin. "And the members of the court do not extract his dart": because it is the cause for the establishment of the dart, it is like a dart. If these members of the court do not extract it, then they themselves have already been pierced—even before the one who holds false views has been pierced. Since this is so, a king or an appointed Brahmin who acts improperly must not be tolerated by the court members, for fear of violating *dharma* and the resulting piercing. (8.12)
Therefore:
"Either the assembly must not enter, or what is appropriate must be spoken.

Or, the members of the court (*sabhyas*) must not accept the authority to adjudicate legal proceedings from the king; or, having accepted that authority, they must speak what is appropriate—that is, the truth—therein. By which—
Whether one speaks or does not speak, a person becomes guilty of sin. || 8.13 ||

Maitreya said: "It is not only by speaking falsely that one becomes a sinner; rather, one becomes so even by remaining silent. Therefore, this man should not be ignored by the members of the assembly, thinking, 'This fellow, acting as the king's agent, does this while looking on, but we ourselves do not. You should not, out of indifference, remain here as if you were free from blame. (8.13)

And so they have said: "Where indeed dharma is [overturned] by adharma— by that which is characterized by the subversion of established order through the lack of established order, such as the approval of contradictions regarding priority, posteriority, and so forth."
Where truth is destroyed by falsehood, through perjured witnesses while the members look on, there the members of the court are themselves slain. (8.14)
Therefore, the members of the court must not remain indifferent; they are not called "members" (sabhyas) merely because they do not act as witnesses. || 8.14 ||
And this being so:
"Dharma alone, when violated, destroys; Dharma, when preserved, preserves.
Therefore, Dharma must not be violated, lest violated Dharma slay us. (8.15)

With this intention, the king's subjects are informed: "This sovereignty has been obtained by you through faith in *dharma*, not through the favor of the king. Therefore, because of these words, one must not destroy *dharma*. Furthermore, from the subsequent verse, "Therefore, one should not violate *dharma*," it follows that this king is a member of the royal class (*rājaprakṛta*), while the members of the assembly (*sabhāsada*) are numerous.

D: Therefore, he ought not to destroy *dharma*. [M: The form *hantumaty* is used; furthermore, from the singular number and the gender in this verse, and from the subsequent verse, "Therefore, one should not neglect *dharma*," it follows that the subject is the king, not the members of the court, because of their plurality. 8.15.
Maitreya said: And because this is the etymological derivation:
"The Blessed One is indeed Dharma, the Bull; he who causes its destruction, the gods know him as a *vṛṣala* (outcaste); therefore, one should not violate Dharma. (8.16)

M.D.: It is not only one of low birth who is a *vṛṣala*; rather, one becomes a *vṛṣala* here through improper action (*vikarman*). This being so, what will your Brahmin caste avail you when you are being swallowed up by unrighteousness due to your transgression? For this reason, this is merely a reproach directed at the Brahmin appointed by the king. (8.16)
M D: This further enumeration is stated for the purpose of defining the duties of the aforementioned Brahmins:
"Dharma alone is the true friend that follows one even unto death;
for everything else indeed goes to destruction along with the body. (8.17)

MD: For this reason, dharma must not be abandoned even out of regard for friends, relatives, and so forth. Otherwise, by neglecting it, there is sin not only for the offender who perceives things wrongly; rather— "A quarter of the demerit falls upon the perpetrator, a quarter reaches the witness, a quarter reaches all the members of the court, and a quarter reaches the king. (8.18)

Therefore, one must not remain indifferent with the thought: "The agent or the witness is connected with the fault; what will happen to us who are neutral? For when an improper legal proceeding is observed, the sin is distributed among all [the parties]. And although there is no distribution of a sin committed by one person among others in general, this principle is demonstrated through an explanatory statement (*arthavāda*) regarding the connection with fault for the purpose of preventing the observation of what is improper. 8.18.
The king becomes [tainted with] sin, yet the members of the assembly are released; the guilt goes to the perpetrator where one deserving of censure is censured. (8.19)

M D: Thus, when right conduct is observed, all this becomes excellent; although this meaning is already implied by the sense [of the preceding], it is restated here due to the inherent nature of the sentence. 8.19.
One who merely lives by his birth may indeed be called a "pseudo-Brahmin" (brāhmaṇabruva) at will;
however, a Śūdra can never be the expounder of dharma to the king. (8.20)

M.D.: This undertaking is intended to establish the eligibility of learned Kṣatriyas and Vaiśyas when a learned Brāhmaṇa appointed by the king is absent; it does not concern those who subsist merely on the basis of their caste. How so? For it has been stated: "Then one should appoint a learned Brāhmaṇa to oversee the affairs. Here, it was said that the mention of the Brāhmaṇa is for the purpose of excluding the other three castes. This being the case, since the exclusion of the Śūdra is already established by that very exclusion, the fact that the Śūdra is excluded again here is understood to be for the purpose of permitting the Kṣatriya and the Vaiśya. For otherwise, the scripture—by such an improper commencement—would become an improper commencement rather than an appropriate one. Otherwise, due to the fault of tautology, it would be an improper commencement. Furthermore, in the absence of a learned Brāhmaṇa, the scripture cannot authorize one who subsists merely on the basis of caste—an unlearned Brāhmaṇa who is incapable of overseeing legal proceedings—because his purpose is lost. Indeed, no one in the world who is blind is authorized to perceive forms. This being the case, this Brāhmaṇa is not excluded by way of an option regarding his absence; rather, this statement is solely for the purpose of exclusion (*paryudāsa*) of one who subsists merely on the basis of caste. And thus, in such sentences, a double negation is observed in common usage: "You may eat even poison, but do not eat in his house. Since there is thus a double negation, the permission for the Kṣatriya and the Vaiśya is established. (8.20)
And this being so— even though he is learned—
if a Śūdra performs the discernment of dharma for a king, [he incurs sin].
[In the place where the Brāhmaṇa has authority...]
