That kingdom sinks away while he looks on, like a cow in the mud. (8.21)

M.D.: This prohibition against Śūdras is for the purpose of praising the appointment of Kṣatriyas and Vaiśyas; this [verse] also was spoken with reference to that very point—[M: the prohibition against Śūdras is not for the purpose of praising the appointment of learned Brāhmaṇas, as it has been stated that this follows from the context]:
"A kingdom in which Śūdras predominate, which is overrun by atheists and devoid of the twice-born, quickly perishes in its entirety, afflicted by famine and disease. (8.22)

M: "Predominantly Śūdra" means that those who instruct in the Dharma are predominantly Śūdras. By the force of this statement, it is understood that such a kingdom becomes overrun by nihilists (nāstika). He states the reason for this: because it is "mostly devoid of the twice-born," meaning it lacks Brāhmaṇas who instruct in the Dharma. And this is logical: a kingdom of this kind perishes. It has already been stated that this verse, like the preceding one, is intended as praise for the appointment of Kṣatriyas and Vaiśyas [not just any Kṣatriyas or Vaiśyas], but not for the appointment of those who are merely so by birth. When the king, being free from distraction, desires to personally oversee legal proceedings, then—
Having occupied the Dharma-seat, with his body properly covered and his mind composed,
he should bow to the world-protectors and begin the examination of legal cases.

The seat for the sake of dharma is the *dharmāsana*. Having sat upon it with his limbs properly covered—this being a restatement (*anuvāda*) of the requirement for modest dress and ornaments through their connection with a previously unstated quality—he should remain composed while examining legal cases. Having paid homage to the guardians of the world (*lokapālas*) depicted in the court paintings or stationed in their respective places, he should commence the investigation of cases by means of speech and mind. This rule regarding the king’s desire to see legal proceedings is intended for visible results; alternatively, it serves as an invisible result (*adṛṣṭārtha*) for the sake of establishing the purposefulness of the treatise. (8.23)
Having understood both profit and loss, as well as merit and demerit in their entirety, he should examine all the legal cases of the litigants according to the order of their castes. (8.24)

The king should perceive that the favor or anger of the realm constitutes gain or loss, and that these are favorable or unfavorable to the administration of the kingdom; furthermore, he should regard merit and demerit in the afterlife as independent of visible results, and thus conduct himself with an observant eye toward his duties. Or rather, he should act having understood that gain and loss are caused by the persistence of enmity or its opposite. And when lawsuits are brought before him, he should attend to them according to the order of castes. It has been stated that "he shall look into the cases of the litigants"; this, moreover, refers specifically to the examination of legal proceedings through inference, since it is for that purpose that it is now being explained.
One should discern the internal disposition of men by external signs:
by their voice, complexion, gestures, appearance, gaze, and movements. (8.25)

Voice (*svara*), complexion (*varṇa*), and gesture (*iṅgita*) constitute "voice, complexion, and gesture" (*svaravarṇeṅgitāni*). Physical appearance (*ākāra*) refers to deformities of the body and the sense organs. These—namely voice, complexion, gesture, and physical appearance—are termed "voice, complexion, gesture, and physical appearance" (*svaravarṇeṅgitākārāḥ*). This designation is made by means of their common and specific characteristics (*sāmānyaviśeṣadharmeṇa*). Among these, "variety" (*vaicitrya*) consists of: (1) vocal deformity (*svaravaikṛtya*), such as stammering and the like; (2) complexion (*varṇa*), which is a change in the form of the limbs; and (3) gesture (*iṅgita*), such as perspiration, trembling, horripilation, and so forth. [One observes] by means of the eyes—that is, through changes in the eyes—and by means of movement (*ceṣṭita*), such as the twitching of hands and eyebrows. Thus, the false speech uttered by the plaintiff, the defendant, or the witnesses is [detected] through the alteration of the voice and other such signs... [At this point, M and D diverge.]

M: ** from *guṇātikrameṇa dharmataḥ parājitya*: this is the final portion of the commentary on 8.58. In M, the folios are misplaced here. The M editor did not notice this; he takes the section for 8.58 from Derrett **.
In M, the remainder of the commentary on 8.25 is given as the final part of the commentary on 8.130.

M: One should understand that even what is to be experienced through direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) is subject to error. This [textual] instruction concerns only the general principle. However, some say that because inference (*anumāna*) is seen to be fallible, the settlement of legal disputes (*vyavahārasthiti*) should depend upon witnesses; but when witnesses are unavailable, one must resort to inference as well. This is improper. If inference is observed to be fallible, then surely the testimony of witnesses is also observed to be so. If you argue that in this case [of witnesses] a decision is reached through an effort at discrimination, then the same will apply to inference and other means of knowledge as well. Furthermore, if inference is fallible, how could one explain why it should be employed for the sake of a decision when witnesses are absent? Therefore, inference is a logically sound instruction. And having established it thus, worldly people employ it even outside of legal proceedings. (8.25)
By means of facial expressions, gestures, gait, movements, and speech, as well as by changes in the eyes and face, the mind within is perceived. (8.26)

M.D.: *Ākāra* is the act of making manifest; it is a transformation of the body and the senses. This is the specific application of that general term. By means of those *ākāras*, which are transformations such as gestures (*iṅgita*) and so forth—wherein "gesture" is as previously described, and here "movement" is added from the preceding verse, as well as any alteration of natural behavior as previously stated, and speech such as stammering as previously stated—and by these transformations of the eyes and face, namely these *ākāras*, gestures, and so forth.

In the world, the intention of another is understood even outside of legal proceedings; likewise, at the time of a legal proceeding, it must be grasped by those authorized to judge—provided they are free from hatred and attachment, and have applied their minds with great care. And thus, this should be understood as the remainder of the preceding verse. (8.26)
The king shall protect the inheritance of a minor heir until he has returned from his teacher's house or until he has passed his childhood. (8.27)

[M adds at the beginning: Because of his excessive compassion, he takes possession of this [wealth] beforehand; and because he takes the inheritance (dāya) due to its connection with the purpose, he is an heir (dāyāda). That which has a child as its owner of the inheritance is "belonging to a minor heir" (bāladāyādaka).]

"Riktha" means ancestral wealth; this is the meaning of the compound. This being so, it follows by implication that he is "without protector" (anātha) because he has neither mother nor father. Therefore, his property should remain under the protection of the king until he has returned from his teacher's house (*samāvṛtta*). His "return," however, is intended to indicate his fitness for worldly transactions (*saṃvyavahāra*). This being the case, even if he is a child who has returned, the king should not hand over the property if he is incapable of managing his own wealth, until he has passed childhood—even if he has not yet returned from his studies. It is stated that one should hand it over only when capacity is present. Because this section concerns the instruction on protecting the property of those without protectors, this other point of a similar nature is now stated. (8.27)

The same protection should be afforded to the daughters of barren women, to those who have no family, and to those who are without religious duties; as well as to women devoted to their husbands, to widows, and to those who are afflicted by illness. (8.28)

The barren woman (*vaśā*) is one who is venerable (*vandya*). A woman whose offspring are female, or one whose offspring are dead—both of these are to be understood by implication as widows (*vidhavā*). A girl without a family (*niṣkulā*) is one who lacks both father and mother. A devoted wife (*pativratā*) is one who does not stray even in the absence of her husband; a widow (*vidhavā*) is one deprived of her husband. [In this context, the term "widow" (*vidhavā*) is understood by implication to include the devoted wife (*pativratā*). If a woman whose husband is away on a journey is not considered a "devoted wife" (*pativratā*) because she is unable to fulfill that role, then a woman whose husband is ill or whose son is ill is not a widow (*avidhavā*) so long as she is still living with her husband. Since those two cases lack the capacity [to maintain the household], the woman who is left without a protector (*anāthā*) is the one intended here. *Note: The commentary clarifies that if a woman whose husband is away is not included under the term "devoted wife," then a woman whose husband is sick or whose son is sick is not a widow as long as the husband is alive; however, because they lack the capacity [to provide for the family], such women are included among those who are "without a protector."*

Or [women] whose sons have gone abroad—or, according to some, whose husbands have gone abroad. Whatever property belongs to these women, whether it be their own *strīdhana* (woman’s property) or the property of their husband, that too must be protected by the king from their own kinsmen. Just as in the case of the property of a minor heir, so too is the protection of the property of those who are destitute a general duty to be performed by the king; such is the instruction. However, a specific teaching regarding those who are destitute is appropriate here for the sake of showing special regard. (8.28)
But if their own kinsmen should seize the property of those women while they are still living,
the righteous lord of the earth shall punish them with the punishment prescribed for thieves.

M.D.: This indicates that, because they are alive, the kinsmen of those who have died shall inherit their wealth according to their proximity. Furthermore, he will later state the distribution of the wealth of one who dies without offspring among the *sapiṇḍas* and others. For this very reason, when there is suspicion of theft, they deserve punishment like thieves. And this other matter, being of such a nature, is mentioned here by way of incidental discussion.
The king shall cause property whose owner has disappeared to be kept for three years;
within three years the owner may take it, but after that period the king shall take it for himself. (8.30)

M.D.: After three years, the king is authorized to enjoy property whose owner has disappeared; this is not a confiscation of it. For it is not proper for him to seize that even after three years once the owner has arrived; indeed, it is impossible to authorize the appropriation of another's property through an interpretation of the meaning that contradicts both logic and scripture. Nor does the statement "the owner may take it back before three years" imply that the owner loses ownership after three years. What then? By the phrase "after [three years] the king may take it," the enjoyment or the act of relinquishment is restated in connection with that [period], due to the inherent nature of the sentence. And this being so, even after three years, having returned—
He who says "this is mine," when questioned according to the rule, and having verified its form, number, and other characteristics, that owner is entitled to the property. (8.31)

M D: When the cause of ownership has been declared, he who does not truly state the place and time of the loss, nor the color, form, and dimensions [of the lost object], deserves a fine equal to its value. 8.32.

In that regard, color consists of white and so forth; shape is the form (*ākāra*) of the color; number, weight, tip, and dimension constitute measurement (*pramāṇa*). And in this context, there is a punishment prescribed as a rule for the purpose of purifying those [transgressions]. (8.32)
Now, remembering the dharma, the king should take a sixth part of lost property that has been recovered, or even a tenth or a twelfth part. 8.33.

M.D.: Even after three years, one should not return everything that has been acquired with its owner present; rather, one should return it after deducting the sixth part or other such share. And the regulation regarding the taking of the sixth part or other shares is determined by the owner's qualities and by the degree of effort expended in guarding the property. (8.33)
Property that has been lost and subsequently found shall remain under the supervision of appointed officials;
whatever thieves the king may catch in that regard, he shall have them executed by means of an elephant.
MD: Because this [elephant] has no owner, this is said for the purpose of protecting it with effort; furthermore, the killing of even disciplined guards is seen to have a practical purpose. (8.34)
If a man should truthfully declare, "This treasure is mine," the king may take a sixth part of it, or even a twelfth. (8.35)

If a person should declare a treasure—whether discovered by the king or not—to be his own on the basis of some reason, a distribution of shares must be determined for him in consideration of his being a Vedic scholar (*śrotriya*) and other such qualities; and in case there is a discrepancy regarding the grounds for his claim:
"But one who speaks falsely shall be fined an eighth part of his own wealth, or a smaller portion calculated from the value of that very treasure. (8.36)

Just as one who is fined according to the measure of his wealth would not fall into despair but would instead accept the disciplinary correction, so should the king cause him to pay that same amount of money. Furthermore, the variation in punishment must be applied with regard to the specific status of the individual. 8.36.
But a learned Brāhmaṇa, having discovered a treasure previously deposited, may take it entirely, for he is the master of all. (8.37)

And this being so, regarding the aforementioned rule "this is mine," there is an optional application (*vikalpena*) of the portion to non-Brāhmaṇas, or else its application to ignorant Brāhmaṇas. (8.37)
But whatever treasure a king may discover buried long ago in the earth,
he should give half of it to the twice-born and deposit the other half in his treasury.
M.D.: This rule regarding the distribution of what has been found belongs to the king; it does not apply to anyone else, due to the force of the statement. 8.38.
For the king is the lord of the earth; by virtue of protecting the ancient treasures and the mineral ores within the ground, he receives a half-share [of their value]. (8.39)

M: [The word *ardhabhāga* means] "one who possesses a share"; for the word *ardha* is seen to denote a "share" as well, as in the expression "the half-share partner and the family friend. This being the case, the determination of the shares must be devised either with regard to the qualities of the observer or according to the king's intention. And thus, the word *ardha* also has the sense of an "equal division. (8.39)
M: At that time, the king must restore to all classes the wealth stolen by thieves;
for a king who makes use of it incurs the guilt of the thief. (8.40)

In this reading, the king should support with his own wealth one whose property has been taken by thieves when it is impossible to recover it; in the reading "recovered from thieves" (*corāhṛtam*), however, the meaning is this: having recovered it from the thieves, the king should not take any portion of it for himself, but should restore it to its rightful place. And thus, both his merit and his fame remain undiminished (or, according to another reading, unrecovered). 8.40.
One who knows the law, having carefully examined the laws of regions and castes, the laws of guilds, and the laws of families, should establish his own duty. (8.41)

The duty pertaining to birth (*jātidharma*) is well known. [Birth refers to being a Brāhmaṇa and so forth, and that is stated to be eternal. [M: Study and so forth are well known among Brāhmaṇas and others. That is stated as an example for the sake of praising the other; D: has *-antatvenocyate*, the rest is broken. Because it is characterized by the scriptures. Local custom (*jānapada*) is conventional (*sāmayika*), not based on scriptural authority, such as the grazing of cattle or the protection of water. The guild-duty (*śreṇīdharma*) is established for the sake of accomplishing their own work by merchants, artisans, and actors. [M: -rakṣaṇādiśreṇīdharmāpati-] The king should also enforce that duty. [M: -prasiddhy-] It is established as follows: "The sale of grain [is forbidden]; or else, for this much time this substance may be sold and this must be purchased," and so forth—this is family custom (*kuladharma*). Regarding immovable property, a convention is established: "One must eat in such-and-such a house; one must not converse with such-and-such a person; he whose transgression occurs [shall be punished]. This conventional duty (*sāmayika dharma*) is to be enforced by the king. One should not disregard it by thinking, "This is merely conventional. And if the king were to show disrespect toward conventions, then, due to the breakdown of order, the law of the fishes (*mātsyanyāya*) would prevail. (8.41)
Men who perform their own duties, remaining established in their respective tasks, become dear to Lakṣmī even though they are far away. (8.42)
M D: This is a praise for the observance of the conventional rules (sāmayika-dharma), intended to inspire enthusiasm. 8.42.
Neither the king himself nor his official should initiate a legal case;
nor should he ever seize property that has not been brought before him by another. (8.43)

The King himself should not initiate a lawsuit out of malice toward any citizen, whether urban or rural, nor out of hatred for a wealthy man, nor out of greed for his property; nor should the King’s appointed judge of legal cases consume the wealth of anyone who has not brought it before the court by any other means whatsoever. Alternatively, another reading is explained: "Nor should he consume by any other means than through legal proceedings the wealth of one who has come before the court. Or yet another reading is explained: "Nor should he consume by any other means than through legal proceedings the wealth of one who has come before the court. For otherwise, through greed, there would be injury to the King in the next world, as well as the visible fault of injury to the administration of the kingdom. But another says: "The King himself should not initiate a case, even if he directly perceives someone committing an improper act; nor should the King's official appointed for that purpose," because the very act of judging legal cases is intended for the determination of victory and defeat. However, the restriction regarding the King is stated: "But [it is] desired by the King. Therefore, there is no fault for him if, having seen an offender himself, he releases him. For if a King were to establish a legal proceeding based on his own conviction alone without a plaintiff, the violation of the administration of the kingdom would follow upon the perception of greed, passion, and hatred. And thus, even if a case is not brought before the court, it should not be seized, even by one equal to Bṛhaspati. For in this way, through pleasing all the people, his fame as a righteous king and his administrative system spread abroad. And thus, even by rejecting witnesses, he should remain the primary authority in legal cases by relying on the purity of the means of knowledge known as inference (*anumāna*), being well-trained in *ānvīkṣikī* (logic). He states an illustration for this in the second half of the preceding verse (8.43).
Just as a hunter traces the track of a deer by drops of blood, so should a king trace the path of dharma through inference. 8.44

And thus, having set aside perception and scripture, one would become one for whom inference is primary in the course of worldly affairs; this is a praise of inference. Since not every object perceptible to the world is a fit subject for logical praise—[for if it were, how could the hand before one's eyes not be a means of valid cognition?]—this praise of inference, which is based on that [perception], namely the previously mentioned "one should discern by external signs," is to be understood as a repudiation of perception and scripture. And so, because of the relationship between the subordinate and the principal, the preceding and following verses are not redundant. Now, regarding worldly affairs, this contemplation of the observer is stated for the purpose of determining the ultimate reality. (8.44)
Established in the procedure of legal proceedings, one should examine the truth, the matter, oneself as the witness, as well as the place, the time, and the form. (8.45)

M D: One should perceive the relative worthiness and insignificance of truth and material gain, making oneself the witness. Likewise, one should consider the abiding of the self in a great place such as heaven through dharma, and the great duration of that stay—or else, the duration of life, which is short here on earth due to being overcome by old age; and the transformation of the self’s form due to the onset of many diseases. Or else, having observed that the form of the inhabitants of heaven—which brings satisfaction to the body and mind, is irreproachable, free from adversaries, and provides unsurpassed enjoyment of pleasure—is the means for attaining heaven, one should abandon material gain and embrace truth. Or else, there is another reading: "One should perceive truth among matters," meaning in legal disputes. This effort of undertaking the rule is for the purpose of prohibiting deception (*chala*). The rest is as previously stated. 8.45.

Whatever has been practiced by the virtuous and by righteous, most excellent twice-born men, that one should establish as not being in conflict with the customs of one's country, family, and caste. (8.46)

By the virtuous (*sadbhiḥ*), who avoid what is forbidden, and by the righteous (*dhārmikaiḥ*), who perform what is enjoined; or else, by the righteous who are virtuous—the word *sat* here has the sense of "existence" (or "being") and is not a redundancy due to the force of the context. By Brāhmaṇas qualified by both attributes. Or else, whatever is practiced by those who are virtuous—meaning possessed of learning and wisdom—and by the righteous—meaning established in the meaning of the scriptures—that one should establish for regions, families, and castes, provided it is not in conflict with the Vedas, the Smṛtis, or the Śāstras. Accordingly, another Smṛti states: "The conduct of the learned (*śiṣṭācāra*) that is not in conflict with the Śāstras is authoritative. But not that which contradicts them, such as the eating of parrots or mainas. And thus, whatever has been practiced by the learned at some time or in some manner, being understood as having a valid purpose, that must be maintained by the king. Or else, this undertaking is for the purpose of instructing regarding the duties of castes, localities, and so forth; for even though these may have visible purposes, they should be performed by the king only when they are not in conflict with the Śāstras, and not those that contradict them. Since [the rule] "the duty of castes and localities" is indeed the remainder of this very verse, its non-redundancy should be understood in this way.

As for what he says: "Or rather, this should be understood as a summary of the preceding; however, the Teacher says that the meaning of this verse is: 'Whatever has been practiced by the virtuous'—whatever is practiced in another region by virtuous, righteous people, provided it is not in conflict with the *Śruti* or another *Smṛti*, the king should establish that even in his own region, and cause those residing in that region to perform it. Likewise, whatever is practiced within a specific family, locality, or time, such as the piercing of the ears and so forth, he should establish that for the entire family. Similarly, whatever custom regarding the time of marriage, the commencement of Vedic study, and so on, has been introduced due to a particular caste, he should establish that for the whole caste. For the sake of ensuring the propagation and stability of these duties through the support of the king, this is stated among the duties of the king. Now begins the procedure for the administration of justice, for which the preliminary definitions have already been established. (8.46)
When urged by the creditor for the sake of recovering the debt, the king shall cause the debtor to pay the amount of the claim that has been proven. 8.47.

The debtor (*adhamaṛṇa*) is one who is at the bottom regarding the debt; who is he? He is the borrower. For what reason? Because he receives that debt along with interest (*sopacaya*) as something to be returned, yet it is difficult to clear and involves much trouble. The creditor (*uttamaṛṇa*), however, is the giver; because he gives back that which is to be received along with interest. And for this reason, he is called "highest" (*uttama*) in relation to the debt being given. This being so, whether the debt has doubled in time or not, when the debtor, being asked for it, does not give that wealth, then, for the sake of its recovery, the king—being urged by the creditor—should cause the debtor to pay the wealth to the creditor, or [the king himself] should pay the debt. This is the general rule for legal procedure (*vyavahāra*). (8.47)
By whatever means a creditor may recover his own wealth, by those very means he should win over and compel the debtor. 8.48.

M.D.: When urged by the creditor, the king should cause the debtor who has acknowledged the debt to pay by means of conciliation and other such methods. This instruction regarding the methods is for the purpose that he should not resort to the destruction of the debtor's livelihood; thus, *dharma* (conciliation) is the first [method]. In this way, because there is no conflict between the two parties, the king’s favor is exercised. These methods for compelling payment have been stated in general; they are now specified in detail. (8.48)
One should recover a debt that has been lent by means of legal process, trickery, customary conduct, and, as the fifth, by force. (8.49)

One should cause [the debtor] to pay gradually by means of righteous persuasion (*dharma*) without causing alarm, or by means of an oath (*śapatha*) once there is agreement. If there is still no compliance even then, one will speak of it through legal procedure (*vyavahāra*). Or, having gained his confidence through various kinds of deception (*chala*); or through customary conduct (*ācarita*), such as sitting at the door of his house during meals and so forth, which is practiced by the world; or through force (*bala*), such as confinement in his own house and so forth, so that there may be no loss of his wealth due to being brought before the king. And this being so, there is no transgression of *dharma* here, because of this—
If a creditor recovers his own wealth from a debtor by his own means, he must not be prosecuted by the king for recovering the money himself. (8.50)

A debtor who commits acts such as locking himself inside his own house should not be prosecuted by the king on the grounds that he is a wrongdoer. As for the creditor, he should be made to accept payment through whatever means are possible, according to the circumstances. But as for the other—the debtor—who denies the debt when it has been proven by evidence, the king shall compel him to pay the amount to the creditor and a small fine according to his ability: "But one who denies a debt which has been proved by evidence, the king shall compel him to pay the amount to the creditor and a small fine according to his ability. (MDh 8.51)
The author will state that for one who denies a debt proven by means of evidence, the fine shall be one-tenth.
Regarding a debt that is admitted, he deserves a fine of five percent;
if it is denied, it is double that—such is the instruction of Manu (MDh 8.139).

This, however, is stated for the purpose of establishing a rule that some form of punishment is to be declared even for one who is virtuous but unable to pay a tenth part of his wealth—or indeed any portion at all—so that he is not simply abandoned on the grounds of being destitute. Furthermore, the means of proof (*karaṇa*) is that which serves as the instrument for determining a matter in doubt; moreover, it is of three kinds. Thus Uśanas recites: "Where there is no written document and no means of proof exists..."
Furthermore, the previously mentioned reproach would not constitute a divine act (*daivī kriyā*) in that case.
Now, since the principles of victory and defeat for the plaintiff and defendant engaged in litigation must be stated, this section is commenced for the purpose of explaining those. 8.51.
When the debtor denies the debt in court upon being told "Pay it," the plaintiff must point out the place [of the transaction] or cite the evidence. (8.52)
[M does not provide the root verse]

Now, the general grounds for victory and defeat for the plaintiff and the defendant engaged in a lawsuit are taught. When a debtor denies a debt that has been received, and is told by the creditor—or by the presiding judge (*prāḍvivāka*)—“Pay! in the assembly at the place of legal proceedings, and not in casual conversation, the accuser (the creditor) shall point out the place of the transaction. Here, the mention of “place” (*deśa*) is by implication intended to indicate witnesses. Thus, the meaning is that he should name those who were present at the time the debt was taken, namely, the persons residing in the court who witnessed the matter being transacted. And this is precisely why [the author] says: “Or he should point out the instrument (*karaṇa*), known as the document, at the very place of legal proceedings. From this it is understood that the mention of “place” is intended to indicate the “instrument”; for the purpose of indicating the witnesses, he should point out either the place or another instrument. Regarding the phrase “one who establishes the debt received,” this is the same meaning as the alternative reading. Alternatively, when the debtor denies the debt and is told by the creditor in the assembly, “Pay! and [the debtor] replies, “It was given by me,” then the accuser (the creditor), being now the one accused by the debtor, shall point out the place. Since the mention of “place” is illustrative, it should also be understood as referring to time: “In what place or at what time was my money returned by you? Or, “Or he should point out the instrument”: he should point out some other instrument that establishes the repayment of the money to you. Or again, the accuser shall point out the “place to be pointed out” (*deśya*); that is, he should describe how it was received. Everything else is the same in both cases. (8.52)
He who points out what should not be pointed out, and he who, having pointed it out, denies it;
and he who does not understand the contradictory meanings of what precedes and follows. (8.53)

"He who points out an improper place to the claimant, or points out an improper object as the subject matter; he who, having pointed it out, then denies it—whether it be a place or the subject matter; and he who does not comprehend the lower and higher points, or other matters such as time, substance, form, and number, which are contradictory in their sequence"—the author will state that "one should designate him as defeated," whether he be the plaintiff or the other party. (8.53)
Furthermore, he who, having stated and then restated his case, subsequently evades it; or who, when questioned about a matter properly set forth, does not accept it; 8.54.

Having pointed to a pretext, or having pointed out a pretext, or having pointed to what is not a pretext—whosoever then evades, or speaks otherwise; that is, having pointed out, "Gold was taken by me from this person," yet in another instance points instead to a son or a servant; when questioned in such a manner by the King or the presiding judge, "At some time or place, did you conduct business with him?"—if, being thus properly questioned, he does not welcome it, thinking, "Let it not be so," because of his failure to perceive the ultimate truth. 8.54.
He who converses privately with witnesses in a place where it is not permitted, or who does not wish to answer when a question is being put to him, or who even walks away; 8.55.

M.D.: If, apart from the assembly hall, he converses privately with witnesses in a secluded place—or speaks with them suddenly and in secret—he too is defeated for fear that the witnesses might be divided. Furthermore, when the witnesses are being questioned, he does not wish for it; under some pretext related to the lawsuit itself, or by demonstrating favor from the king's administration, or at the time of questioning the witnesses, he departs from the place of legal proceedings due to preoccupation with other business, or by showing his service to the king—this has been stated—and because of that, "he is defeated on account of that matter," as the author will say. (8.55)

If, when told "Speak!", he does not speak, or if he fails to clarify what has been said, or if he cannot distinguish between what precedes and what follows, he is defeated on account of that matter. (8.56)

When told "Speak," if he does not speak at the time of the presentation [due to fear of defeat, or because he fails to provide an answer], or if what was spoken is not corroborated by witnesses—either because they are absent, or because of their failure to perceive the intended meaning correctly—he shall lose the case on that account, provided he does not understand the sequence of his own statements, whether those made before the witnesses or elsewhere during the legal proceeding. (8.56)
"If there are witnesses," having said this, he who does not point them out when told "Point them out"—one who stands upon the Dharma should declare him to be devoid of these grounds for proof. (8.57)

M.D.: When a matter cannot be established by means other than witnesses—namely, by those causes that demonstrate the asserted point—in such a case, the witnesses are the refuge... [by the aforementioned causes]. [M: If even those witnesses are not available for one, then the judge seated on the seat of justice, by these aforementioned grounds of defeat, with words of false testimony,] should declare him "defeated" [M: having thus determined him]. Whether it be the plaintiff or the other party, since the grounds for defeat may occur on both sides, the judge, by these means, should declare him "defeated"; this is how the ground of defeat is to be understood. The particle *iti* has the sense of the word *evam* (thus). And so it has been explained.
Now, this is commenced for the purpose of regulating the time for the statements of the plaintiff and the defendant [and the time for their replies]. 8.57.
If the plaintiff does not speak within three fortnights, he shall be punished with a fine according to the law and is defeated in accordance with justice. (8.58)

M D: If the plaintiff does not speak, he shall not cause the lawsuit to be recorded by the king immediately after reporting his own case. In that case, he would be liable for imprisonment and liable for punishment. Depending on the quality of the subject matter of the lawsuit, the application, the option, or the combination of these two [penalties] should be determined. [M: In that case, this person is liable for punishment; it should be understood that the possibility of a lawsuit based on quality exists, and neither the application, the option, nor the combination of these two should be determined merely by reference to the substance.]

By virtue of the word "and" (*ca*), [the punishments of] corporal punishment (*vadha-daṇḍa*) and verbal censure (*vāk-daṇḍa*) are also [included], according to the aforementioned capacity [of the offense], even for those deserving of imprisonment.

In this context, "reversal" (*saṃhava*) is to be understood as occurring through the transgression of the [legal] grounds (*guṇa*), because one who has been defeated according to the law (*dharmataḥ*) may have grounds for appeal (*sopadhatvāt*) due to some other cause; for the plaintiff (*arthin*) must indeed be one whose case is well-established. Now, if he is recognized by some other means of proof (*pramākaraṇa*) as being straightforward (*akuṭila*) because he is without grounds for appeal, then this matter would not be subject to corporal punishment or the like. And so it has been said: "For one defeated regarding the law (*dharma*), there is no other way for the defendant (*pratyarthin*). Now, a time for reply other than the time for the plaintiff is indicated: "If he does not speak within three fortnights," which means he should reply. Therefore, "he is to be bound and punished according to the law" means that having been defeated regarding the law, it is not otherwise. Now, this verse is commenced for the purpose of defining the rule of punishment for the plaintiff or the defendant who has been defeated. (8.58)
